title: Adolescent and Young Adult Medicine Fellowship
prerequisites: Graduate-level biomedical foundations and prior clinical training recommended; this is a knowledge course, not a training prerequisite or admission credential.
Learners should be able to read clinical guidance critically, recognize emergency escalation, and use local supervision/policy; this course does not authorize patient care.
objectives: Synthesize adolescent development, preventive health, psychosocial context, and relationship-centered communication.
Apply source-aligned board-domain knowledge to prevention, reproductive health, behavioral health, nutrition, safety and transition cases.
Identify when screening requires diagnostic assessment, emergency escalation or specialist co-management.
Explain confidentiality, consent and reporting as context- and jurisdiction-dependent.
Interpret population health and quality measures without inferring individual diagnosis.
Distinguish official institutional programme aims, ACGME training requirements, and board eligibility/exam specifications.

units.title: Adolescent development, puberty, and clinical communication
objectives: Explain developmental variation without pathologizing normal diversity.
Use developmentally appropriate, strengths-based interviewing.
Separate chronologic age, pubertal stage, capacity and context.
topics: Physical, cognitive and psychosocial development; puberty; resilience; assent/capacity; strengths-based interview.
boardDomains: Adolescent Medicine
Growth and Development
units.casePractice: Practice a structured developmental history on a fictional adolescent; distinguish red flags from normal variation.
units.assessment: Short-answer developmental formulation scored for biological, psychosocial, and context domains.
units.prerequisites: Medical degree-level biomedical foundations and prior clinical training; learners may use this as independent knowledge review only.

units.title: Routine adolescent health supervision and preventive care
objectives: Construct a private-time plus family-inclusive visit.
Apply age-appropriate preventive guidance and screening without overtesting.
Use a structured psychosocial screen and respond to positive disclosures.
topics: Confidential encounter workflow; HEADSS/HEEADSSS as an interview scaffold not a diagnostic test; preventive visits; immunization; sleep, nutrition, activity, oral health.
boardDomains: Adolescent Medicine
Routine Adolescent Care
units.casePractice: Fictional visit-plan exercise: prioritize preventive concerns, vaccine review and follow-up.

units.title: Consent, confidentiality, ethics, and digital health
objectives: Explain limits before sensitive history.
Identify jurisdiction-specific minor-consent issues for escalation to local counsel/policy.
Recognize EHR, portal, billing and caregiver-access privacy risks.
topics: Private time; assent/capacity; state-law variation; mandatory reporting; imminent safety exceptions; EOBs and portal segmentation.
boardDomains: Adolescent Medicine
Consent and Confidentiality
units.casePractice: Role-play a private-time request and explain a legally variable scenario without giving universal age thresholds.
units.assessment: Rubric: transparent limits, no overpromising privacy, safety/legal escalation, shared decision-making.
units.prerequisites: Medical degree-level biomedical foundations and prior clinical training; learners may use this as independent knowledge review only.

units.title: Sexual and reproductive health, contraception, and pregnancy options

assignment.title: Adolescent-centered continuity and access case conference
assignment.instructions: Analyze an entirely fictional case using public sources. Submit (1) developmental/medical-psychosocial formulation; (2) a confidentiality and safety plan that explicitly flags local-law checks; (3) preventive/reproductive/behavioral care questions and referral boundaries; (4) a transition or community-resource plan; (5) one population-level improvement question with a measure and privacy safeguards. Do not include patient-identifiable information or clinical recommendations for a real person.

rubric.standard: Separates screening from diagnosis; identifies missing data, alternatives and escalation.
Explains limits and explicitly defers to current local law/policy.
Cites primary/authoritative sources and flags old/changed guidance.
Coordinates follow-up and privacy-protective improvement measures.

assignment.passCriteria: 80/100 recommended for this educational assignment only; not a clinical competence or board-passing threshold.

assessment.format: Eight to twelve original single-best-answer questions (10 provided) plus unit checks, fictional case conference, and reflection. No proprietary board questions.
assessment.scoring: Self-study feedback, formative only; no validated psychometric blueprint or criterion standard.
assessment.notice: Not a validated board-passing predictor, official exam content, credential or clinical competence assessment.

topicGaps: At review, 1.2128 verified specialty video hours; 34.7872 hours below the 36-hour target. The only counted video is school/community-system context and does not cover most clinical board domains.
Public SAHM “Beyond the Basics” is described as one-hour lectures, but its recording page requires login; excluded from free public hour totals.
Several SAHM-listed transition videos have public links but durations were not verified; excluded.

Need original or independently verified free public lectures for all units, especially development/routine care, confidentiality, sexual/reproductive health, STIs, mental health, eating disorders, substance use, safety and transition. The 36 planned slots are not published media.

After adding two AAP recordings, the observed free/public video ledger is 2.6958 hours; 33.3042 hours remain below the 36-hour floor. Planned/scripted episode minutes are not recordings or rendered hours.

Unit 4–5 recordings add communication and reproductive-health teaching, but do not substitute for current, detailed clinical guideline instruction. The linked CDC adolescent STI page is explicitly a 2021 source; re-check updates before clinical use.

No duration-verified free public recordings were added for developmental formulation, eating disorders, substance use, violence/safeguarding, suicide-risk disposition, or chronic-disease transition. The authored episodes are limited original scripts, not full fellow training.

The SAHM Beyond the Basics lecture series advertises one-hour sessions, but its recording access section requires a SAHM portal login; these recordings remain excluded from this open-access counted ledger.

The CHOC adolescent gynecology and abnormal uterine bleeding archive entries are relevant candidates, but the catalog/article fetch did not expose an independently observed runtime; they are not counted pending player-level duration verification.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP)
American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM)
American Board of Family Medicine (ABFM)
medical.boardStatus: There is a joint Adolescent Medicine certifying examination developed with ABP, ABIM and ABFM and administered by ABP (ABIM route described as joint). ABFM offers an Adolescent Medicine Certificate of Added Qualification pathway and continuing certification by longitudinal assessment. This is a real physician clinical subspecialty/fellowship, not a generic directory category, research-only job, non-physician supplement, or combined residency. MGBfC is described by its official page as newly created; its current ACGME accreditation/status and detailed pathway-specific eligibility are not independently established here. A separate examination route is evidenced by the board sources; exact candidate route varies by primary specialty and board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Only the relevant board determines eligibility. ABP page (checked 2025-11-25) specifies primary ABP Pediatrics, ABIM Internal Medicine or ABFM Family Medicine certification, and for its ABP route three years of ACGME/RCPSC-accredited adolescent-medicine fellowship plus board-specific requirements. ACGME requirements effective 2026-07-01 prescribe a minimum 36 months for pediatrics graduates and 24 months for FM/IM graduates. Completion of this independent course, or any MGB/BCH programme listing alone, does not confer eligibility or certification. Confirm current rules with the relevant board.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A healthy 16-year-old attends a preventive visit with a parent. What is the best first step before sensitive questions?

options.text: Promise absolute confidentiality for everything disclosed.
Explain the usual private-time practice and its safety/legal limits, then invite the parent to step out.
Conduct the entire visit only with the parent.
Ask sensitive questions in the waiting room.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP supports routine private time while explaining that confidentiality has legal and safety limits; do not promise absolute confidentiality, and requirements vary by jurisdiction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 17-year-old has a positive ASQ suicide-risk screen in outpatient care. Which response best follows NIMH pathway principles?

options.text: Treat the screen as a definitive diagnosis and start medication immediately.
Ignore the result unless a parent confirms it.
Arrange a brief suicide safety assessment by a trained clinician, then determine disposition using the setting’s pathway.
Send the youth home without discussion because screening is not diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIMH describes a three-tier pathway: brief screen, brief safety assessment after positive screen, then disposition. Screening alone neither diagnoses nor resolves risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: A sexually active 20-year-old woman asks for routine prevention. Which screening approach is most consistent with CDC adolescent/young adult guidance?

options.text: Annual chlamydia and gonorrhea screening, with additional sites guided by reported exposure and shared decision-making.
Only screen if symptoms occur.
Screen every adolescent for every STI regardless of age, behavior, or exposure.
Cervical cancer screening must begin in all adolescents at sexual debut.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC recommends annual chlamydia and gonorrhea screening for sexually active females younger than 25 years and exposure-informed extragenital testing; screening varies by infection and risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 15-year-old is interested in contraception. Which counseling principle is best?

options.text: Recommend one method without discussing preferences.
Offer noncoercive information about suitable methods and correct use, and discuss condoms for STI prevention and jurisdiction-specific consent/privacy.
Tell the teen that long-acting contraception is prohibited for minors.
Discuss pregnancy prevention but not STIs.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC promotes comprehensive person-centered counseling, method choice, correct use and condom use for STI prevention. Legal consent and confidentiality details are location-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 17-year-old with a chronic condition will transfer to adult care in several months. What is the strongest transition plan?

options.text: Transfer the chart on the birthday and end follow-up.
Use readiness goals, support self-management, create a portable summary, arrange a warm handoff and confirm connection.
Require complete independent self-management before discussing transfer.
Wait until age 21 to discuss transition.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SAHM transition objectives stress preparation over time, readiness assessment, defined core elements and measurable outcomes; chronic illness calls for coordinated medical-home continuity.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 15-year-old with restrictive eating symptoms has a BMI in a population range often called normal. What is the best reasoning?

options.text: Normal-range BMI excludes clinically important eating pathology.
Assess trajectory, symptoms, vital signs, medical stability, nutrition and psychosocial context; do not let body size alone rule out risk.
Diagnose solely from one laboratory result.
Delay evaluation until weight falls below a fixed cutoff.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adolescent eating disorders may present across body sizes; safety requires assessment of trajectory, symptoms and physiologic/psychosocial status, not a single BMI cutoff.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teen discloses violence in a confidential interview. Which response is best?

options.text: Promise never to disclose any information.
Use a nonjudgmental trauma-informed response, assess immediate safety, explain any limits and follow local reporting requirements with appropriate support.
Confront the alleged perpetrator before the visit ends.
End the interview to protect confidentiality.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Privacy and safety coexist; clinicians should explain confidentiality limits, assess urgent safety, and apply local law/mandated-reporting and team pathways.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teaching committee uses a board content outline to design this self-study curriculum. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The ABP itself states the content outline is a complete curriculum and clinical competency assessment.
The content outline organizes exam domains and relative weighting, but it is not a complete curriculum or skills assessment.
Every fellowship must teach exactly the same sequence of lectures.
Completion of this independent course makes a participant board-eligible.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP explicitly distinguishes exam outlines from curricula and notes that important trainee skills may not be tested in MCQ format. Independent study does not create eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A young patient reports a same-day overdose in the home but is alert and asks that no one be told. What is the priority?

options.text: Keep all information confidential without assessing anyone else.
Prioritize immediate safety and appropriate emergency response, explain relevant confidentiality limits, and involve the right supports under law and policy.
Focus first on routine preventive care.
Wait for the next appointment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Acute life-threatening safety concerns require immediate action and appropriate emergency/supervisory escalation; the exact reporting/disclosure basis depends on situation and law.

practiceQuestions.stem: A question asks whether any 3-year adolescent-medicine fellowship is required for every physician board pathway. What is the precise answer?

options.text: Yes; ACGME requires three years for all entrants.
No; ACGME specifies at least 24 months for family- and internal-medicine graduates, and 36 months for pediatrics graduates; board-specific rules still apply.
No training is required if the candidate completes online courses.
Duration depends only on employer preference.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Effective 2026 ACGME requirements distinguish minimum program length by prior discipline. ABP eligibility specifically calls for a 3-year pediatrics route. Verify the relevant board and pathway; education cannot confer eligibility.

title: Foot and Ankle Surgery Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (post-residency orthopaedic surgery fellowship; ACGME subspecialty framework; MGB merger scheduled to begin with inaugural class August 2028)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.recommended: Senior orthopaedic surgery resident/fellow or practicing orthopaedic surgeon with foundational anatomy, MSK examination, imaging, fracture principles and evidence appraisal. Open educational access does not verify qualifications.
prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate physician self-study; nonclinical learning only.
prerequisites.notPrerequisite: No patient contact, clinical placement, operative practice, proctoring or credential is provided.

objectives: Organize evaluation and differential diagnosis across ankle/leg, hindfoot, midfoot, forefoot and general foot/ankle conditions.
Interpret the published ABOS 2025 Foot and Ankle practice-profiled recertification blueprint accurately without misrepresenting it as initial board certification.
Compare evidence-informed nonoperative and operative option families, their risks, alternatives and uncertainty.
Recognize urgent limb-threatening and systemic red flags and identify the need for qualified clinical escalation.
Appraise open clinical guidelines, primary research and case-based educational material with attention to update date and rights.
Explain clearly the boundary between education and supervised clinical/operative competence.

units.title: Framework, anatomy, mechanics, gait and evidence-based reasoning
objectives: Use a reproducible history and focused foot/ankle examination, including neurovascular, skin, alignment and gait elements.
Interpret weight-bearing radiographs and select advanced imaging only when it changes a decision.
Use outcomes, uncertainty and patient goals to compare conservative and operative options.
topics: foot/ankle functional anatomy; hindfoot/midfoot/forefoot; gait and load transfer; Ottawa-style injury assessment; radiograph views/alignment; CT/MRI/US indications; shared decisions; evidence appraisal
boardDomains: General 16%: biomechanics/gait, orthoses/bracing, pharmacology/metabolic, pain; all anatomic domains
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional examination patterns; review image-based Northwestern foot/ankle teaching cases by link only.
units.assessment: Structured examination and imaging justification; rubric: 40% completeness, 30% anatomy/alignment, 20% test selection, 10% uncertainty/communication.

units.title: Nonoperative care, orthoses, footwear, pharmacology and perioperative safety
objectives: Match offloading, footwear, bracing, rehabilitation and medication to pathology and patient context.

Critically discuss perioperative VTE and antibiotic evidence, including uncertainty.
topics: orthoses/shoe modification; immobilization; rehabilitation; NSAID/steroid/fluoroquinolone cautions; osteoporosis and vitamin D; smoking, diabetes, nutrition; VTE risk; infection prevention; consent and safety
boardDomains: General: orthotics/bracing 2%, pharmacology/metabolic 2%, DVT/PE 1%, CRPS 1%
units.casePractice: Fictional adult with painful ankle OA and diabetes: build non-operative option matrix, no treatment directive.
units.assessment: Written plan matrix; rubric: 35% fit to diagnosis, 25% risk/contraindications, 20% evidence, 20% shared decision-making.

units.title: Forefoot: hallux valgus/rigidus, lesser toes and metatarsalgia
objectives: Distinguish common forefoot deformity patterns and relevant differential diagnoses.

Compare non-operative and procedure-family rationales and complications at a conceptual level.

boardDomains: Forefoot 22%: hallux valgus 5%, hallux rigidus 2%, lesser toes 2%, bunionette, neuroma, MTP instability and other listed categories
units.casePractice: Use the linked BOFAS hallux valgus lecture to outline decision variables; do not copy its case images.
units.assessment: Short oral-style differential and procedure-choice rationale; rubric: 40% diagnosis, 30% structural reasoning, 20% alternatives/risks, 10% citations.

units.title: Adult acquired flatfoot/PCFD, cavovarus and neuromuscular deformity
objectives: Characterize flexibility, alignment, tendon function and neurologic context in flatfoot and cavovarus.
Use clinical and imaging features to form a staged differential and describe broad treatment principles.
Identify when deformity reflects neuropathy, coalition, inflammatory disease or other secondary cause.
topics: progressive collapsing foot deformity; posterior tibial tendon dysfunction; flexible/rigid flatfoot; cavovarus; CMT; spasticity; coalition; tendon transfer concepts; external fixation overview
boardDomains: Hindfoot 26%: flatfoot 5%, cavovarus/CMT/spasticity 3%, coalition, accessory navicular; biomechanics/general
units.casePractice: Linked BOFAS cavus/planus recordings plus fictional flexible-versus-rigid comparison.
units.assessment: Annotated alignment worksheet; rubric: 35% classification, 30% differential, 20% management logic, 15% limits/uncertainty.

units.title: Ankle sprain, syndesmosis, chronic instability and osteochondral lesions
objectives: Differentiate lateral, medial and syndesmotic injury patterns using history, examination and appropriate imaging.

Compare rehabilitation and operative decision factors without procedural instruction.
topics: ankle sprain; chronic instability; syndesmosis; deltoid complex; osteochondral lesion of talus; ankle impingement; sports foot/ankle; return-to-activity evidence
boardDomains: Ankle/leg 28%: ankle instability/sprain 3%, syndesmosis 2%, osteochondral lesions 2%, impingement, tendon injury

units.title: Ankle, talus and hindfoot trauma
objectives: Classify ankle, pilon, talar, calcaneal and hindfoot injuries and flag time-critical threats.
Reason through soft-tissue status, staged care and imaging in high-energy injury at a conceptual level.
Recognize compartment syndrome, open injury, neurovascular compromise and complications.
topics: ankle fracture; syndesmosis; posterior malleolus; pilon; talus neck/body/process; calcaneus; hindfoot dislocation; stress injury; fracture in neuropathy; compartment syndrome
boardDomains: Ankle/leg: fracture 4%, pilon 1%, stress injuries, compartment syndrome; Hindfoot: calcaneus 3%, talus 3%, dislocations, tarsal fracture
units.casePractice: Discuss recorded BOFAS pilon and foot-compartment cases; source use only, no images exported.
units.assessment: Prioritization and imaging oral defense; rubric: 35% urgency/safety, 30% classification, 20% soft tissue/staging reasoning, 15% complications.

units.title: Achilles and other tendon disorders
objectives: Distinguish acute Achilles rupture from tendinopathy and other posterior ankle pain causes.
Describe evidence-informed nonoperative/operative decision factors and rehabilitation outcomes.
Recognize tendon-transfer concepts and peroneal/anterior tibial tendon pathology.
topics: Achilles rupture; insertional/midsubstance tendinopathy; gastrocnemius contracture/tear; peroneal tears; tibialis anterior; posterior tibial tendon; tendon transfer; rehabilitation and rerupture
boardDomains: Ankle/leg tendon tears and Achilles domains; hindfoot heel pain; forefoot as relevant
units.casePractice: Compare fictional acute rupture with chronic tendon pain; cite the AOFAS acute rupture position statement.
units.assessment: Evidence summary and differential; rubric: 30% discrimination, 30% evidence, 20% risk/rehab, 20% calibrated recommendation.

units.title: Ankle arthritis: evaluation and shared-choice treatment
objectives: Differentiate post-traumatic, primary and inflammatory arthritis and identify important mimics.
Use alignment, adjacent joints, bone stock, soft-tissue, activity and patient goals to frame options.
Compare joint preservation, arthrodesis and total ankle arthroplasty evidence and limitations.
topics: ankle OA; weight-bearing alignment; ankle fusion; total ankle arthroplasty; joint preservation; adjacent joint disease; infection exclusion; complications and revision
boardDomains: Ankle/leg arthritis (arthroplasty/arthrodesis) 4%; hindfoot arthritis 3%; general metabolic/inflammatory
units.casePractice: View BOFAS ankle arthritis lectures and construct a preference-sensitive option table, not patient advice.
units.assessment: Two-page decision memo; rubric: 30% disease/context, 30% valid alternatives, 25% evidence/uncertainty, 15% communication.

units.title: Midfoot, hindfoot and forefoot arthritis; fusion principles and complications
objectives: Localize symptomatic joint disease and separate structural imaging changes from pain generators.
Reason about fusion extent at conceptual level, adjacent-joint mechanics and patient-specific tradeoffs.
Recognize nonunion, malalignment, wound, hardware, infection and persistent-pain risks.
topics: midfoot OA; hindfoot arthritis; triple arthrodesis; subtalar/talonavicular/midfoot fusion concepts; hallux rigidus; inflammatory arthritis/gout; nonunion; revision
boardDomains: Hindfoot arthritis 3%; Midfoot arthritis 2%; forefoot hallux rigidus 2%; general inflammatory conditions/gout 2%
units.casePractice: A 63-year-old case is discussed in BOFAS hindfoot/midfoot lecture; listen to source, note source does not attest re-use rights or de-identification.
units.assessment: Complication-focused case conference; rubric: 30% localization, 30% alternatives/extent logic, 25% complication prevention, 15% evidence.

units.title: Diabetic foot, Charcot neuroarthropathy, ulceration and limb preservation
objectives: Separate acute Charcot changes, infection, ulcer-related bone infection and fracture in neuropathic foot.
Describe multidisciplinary assessment, offloading and limb-preservation decision variables.
Use current diabetes and IWGDF guidance for questions while acknowledging local practice variation.
topics: neuropathy and vascular assessment; Charcot; diabetic fracture; ulcer; infection; osteomyelitis; offloading; limb salvage versus amputation; glycemic and skin risk
boardDomains: Midfoot Charcot 3%; ankle diabetic fracture/Charcot 2%; forefoot diabetic complications 2%; general metabolic/infection/amputation
units.casePractice: Use BOFAS public diabetic foot recordings; no rehosting. Pair with IWGDF guideline for fictional scenario.
units.assessment: Multidisciplinary referral map and evidence critique; rubric: 30% risk triage, 30% infection/ischemia differential, 25% options, 15% team/safety.

units.title: Infection, tumors, neuropathy, pain and general complications
objectives: Develop a safe differential for acute infection, puncture wound, mass, nerve entrapment and chronic pain.
Identify red flags needing timely specialty assessment and appropriate work-up.
Discuss biopsy/referral principles and limits; avoid treating an undiagnosed mass as benign.
topics: septic arthritis/osteomyelitis; surgical site infection; puncture wound; tumor and mimics; peroneal/tarsal tunnel neuropathy; CRPS; DVT/PE; amputation; pharmacology/osteoporosis
boardDomains: General 16%: infection/puncture/amputation 3%, tumor 2%, nerve, DVT/PE, CRPS, metabolic and pharmacology
units.casePractice: Linked BOFAS infection and tumor teaching lectures; case image viewing only, no copying.
units.assessment: Red-flag written-viva; rubric: 35% differential, 30% escalation/work-up, 20% risk, 15% limits.

units.title: Pediatric and special populations, research, quality and longitudinal follow-up
objectives: Recognize age-sensitive differential diagnoses, growth and skeletal maturity issues and referral needs.
Evaluate outcomes evidence, study design, registries and complication reporting.
Plan longitudinal follow-up and explain the boundary between self-study and supervised operative competence.
topics: pediatric deformity; coalition; growth; disability; older adults; patient-reported outcomes; evidence appraisal; quality improvement; recurrence/revision; mentorship, ethics and scope
boardDomains: Hindfoot coalition/accessory navicular; General biomechanics/metabolic/pain; longitudinal evidence domains
units.casePractice: Compare linked pediatric BOFAS lecture with Northwestern pediatric/ankle case index; use link only, no exports.
units.assessment: Critical appraisal and reflective scope statement; rubric: 35% evidence appraisal, 25% developmental context, 20% outcome/follow-up, 20% safety/scope.

assignment.title: Integrated foot-and-ankle case portfolio (fictional educational cases)
assignment.instructions: Complete one structured case analysis for each region (ankle/leg, hindfoot, midfoot, forefoot, general), plus a literature appraisal. State the differential; identify missing information; justify imaging; compare nonoperative and operative option families; discuss risks, follow-up and uncertainty. Do not write patient-specific orders or procedural steps. Use only linked public cases and no copied patient images.

rubric.criterion: Problem representation, differential and red flags
Option comparison, risks and longitudinal outcome
Ethics, uncertainty, source quality and scope boundaries

assignment.passRule: Suggested formative threshold 70/100 with mandatory remediation for missed red flags; this is a local educational rubric, not a validated board-passing predictor.

assessment.format: 12 unit quizzes (10 original items each) and 5 regional case vivas plus capstone portfolio; formative self-study only.
assessment.domains: Crosswalk to ABOS 2025 Foot and Ankle Practice-Profiled Recertification blueprint, which is a maintenance blueprint. It is not an initial ABOS certification blueprint.
assessment.rubric: Assess accurate localization, differential, investigation choice, evidence-quality appraisal, options/risks, and calibrated uncertainty; give no credit for procedural confidence unsupported by supervised skill.
assessment.limitations: Questions and assessments are original and educational; not official ABOS content, validated predictor, or guarantee of passing.

studyHours.plan: Twelve units at approximately 14 hours each (recorded video viewing, free reading, note-making, original quizzes and case reasoning). This is a self-study planning estimate, not observed lecture time, fellowship duration or exam-readiness evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A runner has months of lateral ankle pain after repeated inversion episodes. Examination and radiographs are described, but MRI is not yet obtained. Which reasoning step is most defensible before selecting treatment?

options.text: Assume isolated lateral ligament insufficiency and book reconstruction.
Assess instability, alignment, peroneal tendons, cartilage and associated pathology; select further imaging only if it changes management.
Treat all chronic ankle pain as an osteochondral lesion.
Order CT arthrography for every recurrent sprain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Chronic symptoms may reflect ligament laxity plus alignment, tendon, cartilage or other pathology. A focused examination and targeted imaging precede an individualized plan; no one imaging test is universal.
practiceQuestions.domain: Ankle instability, osteochondral lesions, diagnostic reasoning

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a closed displaced pilon fracture has marked swelling and threatened soft tissues. Which principle best describes the educational priority?

options.text: Apply the same immediate definitive fixation regardless of soft-tissue condition.
Prioritize urgent limb/soft-tissue assessment and choose staged management based on injury and soft tissues.
Ignore neurovascular status if pulses are present.
Delay all assessment until swelling resolves.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pilon fractures can be high-energy injuries with severe soft-tissue risk; safety evaluation, neurovascular assessment and soft-tissue-informed staging are fundamental. This is a principle, not procedural instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which pair correctly states the 2025 ABOS Foot and Ankle recertification blueprint weights?

options.text: Ankle/leg 28%, hindfoot 26%.
Ankle/leg 50%, hindfoot 10%.
Forefoot 40%, general 5%.
Midfoot 26%, general 8%.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 ABOS practice-profiled recertification blueprint lists ankle/leg 28%, hindfoot 26%, midfoot 8%, forefoot 22%, general 16%.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has symptomatic ankle osteoarthritis and asks about fusion versus total ankle arthroplasty. Which answer best reflects evidence-informed counseling?

options.text: The same procedure is best for every patient.
Compare diagnosis, alignment, bone/soft-tissue status, adjacent joints, activity, goals and risks; explain uncertainty and alternatives.
Arthroplasty eliminates future revision risk.
Fusion always prevents adjacent-joint symptoms.

practiceQuestions.rationale: No universal procedure choice follows from arthritis alone. Current guidance supports individualized trade-off discussion; neither procedure guarantees a particular outcome or eliminates later problems.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a person with diabetes and sensory loss, a warm swollen foot after minor trauma is being assessed. Which approach is safest educationally?

options.text: Assume infection; omit vascular and skin assessment.
Consider Charcot, fracture, infection and other causes; assess skin, perfusion, neuropathy and imaging in a multidisciplinary context.
Prescribe unrestricted weight bearing.
Use one radiograph to exclude all early neuropathic disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Neuropathic diabetic foot presentations require a differential including Charcot neuroarthropathy, fracture and infection and assessment of ulcer, vascular and systemic features. Guideline-directed clinical assessment is essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A painful midfoot has radiographic arthrosis at more than one joint. What best prevents overinterpreting the image?

options.text: Treat every abnormal joint as symptomatic.
Correlate pain localization, examination, weight-bearing alignment and selective diagnostic work-up with the patient’s functional goals.
Choose the largest fusion construct from radiographs alone.
Ignore adjacent joint biomechanics.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiographic change does not automatically identify the pain generator. Correlating symptoms, exam and loaded imaging supports reasoned option selection and avoids over-treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient presents with acute ankle injury and pain out of proportion, progressive swelling and tense compartments. Which is the most important next conceptual priority?

options.text: Reassure based on a normal initial radiograph.
Urgently evaluate for compartment syndrome and limb threat; do not delay escalation for routine outpatient imaging.
Wait for bruising to appear.
Assume complex regional pain syndrome.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Compartment syndrome is a limb-threatening emergency. Appropriate urgent assessment/escalation is necessary; early imaging does not rule it out. This educational item is not an emergency protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about orthopaedic foot-and-ankle credentials is correct?

options.text: A fellowship certificate alone creates ABOS subspecialty board certification in foot and ankle.
ABOS lists hand and orthopaedic sports medicine subspecialty certificates; its Foot/Ankle practice-profiled examination is a recertification option and is not a new initial subspecialty certificate.
ABFAS and ABOS are interchangeable boards.
AOFAS match listing proves ABOS board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS distinguishes primary orthopaedic certification, listed subspecialty certificates, and practice-profiled recertification examinations. Podiatric ABFAS is a separate certifying route and not interchangeable with ABOS.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with Achilles pain has chronic insertional symptoms. Which reasoning is best before a treatment recommendation?

options.text: Label every posterior heel pain as acute tendon rupture.
Distinguish insertional from midsubstance disease, rupture and alternative causes; consider patient factors and current evidence.
Recommend immediate surgery in all cases.
Avoid examining tendon function.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A careful history/examination and differential determine whether this is tendinopathy, rupture or another process. Procedure choice should follow current evidence and context, not a universal rule.

practiceQuestions.stem: A small painful foot mass is referred with a presumed benign diagnosis but no adequate work-up. What is the safest educational principle?

options.text: Excise it without establishing diagnosis.
Use appropriate evaluation and referral; do not assume a mass is benign or perform unplanned excision.
Use radiographs alone to exclude all soft-tissue tumors.
Delay evaluation until symptoms resolve.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Foot and ankle tumors have benign and malignant differentials. Careful evaluation/referral and avoidance of unplanned excision protect diagnostic options.

assignment.title: Longitudinal case conference dossier (fictional composite only)
assignment.instructions: Choose one fictional life-stage scenario spanning neurology and reproductive health. Submit (1) an inclusive history/problem representation; (2) prioritized differential with emergency red flags; (3) source-dated evidence table using at least two current authoritative primary sources; (4) multidisciplinary roles and patient-centered questions; (5) a one-page plan that explicitly avoids issuing real patient orders; and (6) a 300-word reflection on uncertainty, evidence gaps and equity. Do not submit real patient data/images.

rubric.meets: Prioritized, life-stage aware, separates observed facts from inference, identifies red flags.
Uses current authoritative sources, dates them, notes gated/outdated resources and supports claims.
Patient goals, inclusive language, clear team roles and appropriate escalation.

Readable, privacy-protective and uses case links/visual rights lawfully.

assessment.limitation: Not an official examination, competence assessment, board predictor or certification.

topicGaps: Four unique public full recordings now have directly observed player durations: 3.1458 hours total (3 hours 8 minutes 45 seconds); the 36-hour verified-video floor remains short by 32.8542 hours (32 hours 51 minutes 15 seconds). The added original scripts are not recorded videos and do not reduce this ledger gap.

The two new free recordings strengthen menstrual/catamenial epilepsy, contraception and pregnancy domains, but do not provide sufficient depth for current individualized antiseizure pharmacology, complex contraception eligibility, pregnancy/postpartum medication monitoring, lactation, or neurodevelopmental outcomes.

No exact-duration, unrestricted full recording was verified for MS disease-modifying treatment around pregnancy/lactation, detailed maternal-stroke systems, postpartum headache secondary-cause workup, menopause/midlife, or collaborative clinical electives. Public candidate pages/transcripts remain uncounted where duration/access could not be verified.

The CDC U.S. MEC source page did not extract in stateless access during this review, so no category-level contraceptive recommendation is taught or keyed. ACOG clinical guidance is member/subscriber restricted; its public landing page is used only to establish subject scope and currency notices.

The named fellowship remains institutional clinical training, not a separate ABPN exam. ABPN Neurology remains the relevant parent specialty; women’s-neurology-specific exam blueprint was not found. Broad parent-domain mapping is not a claim of complete blueprint coverage.

A full 36 hours of relevant, free, accessible and duration-observed video was not found. Do not infer clinical competence or target attainment from source plans, reading hours, scripted episodes, or study-workload estimates.

boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) — Neurology (primary specialty certification)
medical.boardStatus: The MGB women’s neurology fellowship is an institutional clinical fellowship in an emerging focus area. ABPN’s current public examination pages list Neurology primary certification and recognized subspecialty examinations, but do not list a separate Women’s Neurology examination. The appropriate board framework here is broad ABPN Neurology content, not a separate women’s neurology blueprint. Fellowship completion does not itself grant ABPN certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The MGB public programme page says applicants should have completed an ACGME-accredited neurology residency and be board eligible or certified in neurology. Verify the current ABPN requirements directly.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham (Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, as named on programme page)
officialProgrammes.name: MGB Women’s Neurology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a clinical physician fellowship: supervised experience and formal instruction; longitudinal ambulatory headache, epilepsy, stroke, MS, general neurology and obstetrical neurology clinics; two months electives including women’s mental health, maternal-fetal medicine, functional neurologic disorders, prenatal genetics, neuroendocrinology, mitochondrial disorders, obstetric anesthesia, midlife health, contraception, connective tissue/autoimmune disorders; variable research component. It requires ACGME-accredited neurology residency and neurology board eligibility or certification. It does not publish a complete syllabus, rotation-hour breakdown, case volume or separate board examination.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Institution/programme claims taken from the official MGB fellowship page and its stated hosting institutions. No directory category is treated as accreditation. The page describes clinical physician training plus research; it does not make the research component a separate program or non-physician supplement. The item is not a combined residency/fellowship. No independent ACGME accreditation status for this named program was established in this review.
sourceCaveats: No complete official institutional curriculum, didactic schedule, longitudinal case counts or rotation-hour allocation was found on the public MGB page.
ACOG’s public landing page is readable but explicitly says its clinical guidance is member/subscriber content; linked PDF free access is not confirmed.
CDC U.S. MEC page was identified but stateless extraction failed. Its current classification should be checked directly before clinical use; no granular category is used as a keyed answer.
ABPN exam requirements change; linked current page should be checked. Fellowship and course do not confer board eligibility.
Two YouTube durations were read from public player displays via stateless fetch; watch availability and runtimes may change. Video licenses permit platform viewing, not rehosting.

Published case reports are link-only resources. No clinical image or patient record was copied. Free-to-view is not permission to reproduce; independent image rights/de-identification review remains necessary.

This course is independent and unaffiliated with MGB, Harvard Medical School, ABPN, AAN, ACOG or AHA. Human clinical review not performed. No accredited clinical training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence, certificate, diagnosis or guaranteed examination result.

topicGaps: Four unique public full recordings now have directly observed player durations: 3.1458 hours total (3 hours 8 minutes 45 seconds); the 36-hour verified-video floor remains short by 32.8542 hours (32 hours 51 minutes 15 seconds). The added original scripts are not recorded videos and do not reduce this ledger gap.

The two new free recordings strengthen menstrual/catamenial epilepsy, contraception and pregnancy domains, but do not provide sufficient depth for current individualized antiseizure pharmacology, complex contraception eligibility, pregnancy/postpartum medication monitoring, lactation, or neurodevelopmental outcomes.

No exact-duration, unrestricted full recording was verified for MS disease-modifying treatment around pregnancy/lactation, detailed maternal-stroke systems, postpartum headache secondary-cause workup, menopause/midlife, or collaborative clinical electives. Public candidate pages/transcripts remain uncounted where duration/access could not be verified.

The CDC U.S. MEC source page did not extract in stateless access during this review, so no category-level contraceptive recommendation is taught or keyed. ACOG clinical guidance is member/subscriber restricted; its public landing page is used only to establish subject scope and currency notices.

The named fellowship remains institutional clinical training, not a separate ABPN exam. ABPN Neurology remains the relevant parent specialty; women’s-neurology-specific exam blueprint was not found. Broad parent-domain mapping is not a claim of complete blueprint coverage.

A full 36 hours of relevant, free, accessible and duration-observed video was not found. Do not infer clinical competence or target attainment from source plans, reading hours, scripted episodes, or study-workload estimates.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with epilepsy who plans pregnancy asks whether to stop an antiseizure medication immediately after a positive home test. Which response best reflects the current AAN/AES/SMFM guideline approach?

options.text: Advise abrupt cessation of all antiseizure therapy.
Explain that medication decisions require prompt discussion with the treating neurologist and pregnancy-care team; do not stop abruptly without clinical guidance.
State that every antiseizure medicine has identical fetal risk.
Defer discussion until after delivery.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2024 guideline addresses medication exposure and outcomes in people with epilepsy of childbearing potential. A safe educational response is prompt coordinated review, not abrupt unsupervised withdrawal or delay.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the 2024 AAN/AES/SMFM pregnancy guideline?

options.text: It certifies physicians in women’s neurology.
It addresses effects of antiseizure medications and folic acid on congenital, perinatal and neurodevelopmental outcomes.
It replaces the ABPN neurology examination.
It establishes that all seizure medications can be stopped during pregnancy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAN page describes the guideline scope as antiseizure medication and folic acid supplementation outcomes; it does not define an examination or universal stop rule.

practiceQuestions.stem: A postpartum patient reports a sudden, severe headache that is new for her. What is the best initial reasoning stance?

options.text: Assume migraine because pregnancy commonly causes headache.
Treat the new or markedly changed postpartum headache as requiring assessment for secondary causes and urgent red flags.
Avoid neurologic evaluation until the postpartum period ends.
Reassure if there is no known migraine history.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACOG’s guideline covers primary and secondary headaches during pregnancy and postpartum. New or changed headache calls for structured evaluation; emergencies must not be dismissed as primary headache.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about maternal stroke is supported by the AHA’s January 2026 public summary?

options.text: Pregnancy should delay evidence-based acute stroke treatment.
Pregnancy-associated stroke is rare but potentially life-threatening; pregnancy should not delay evidence-based treatment of acute stroke.
Stroke risk is zero in postpartum patients.
Only thromboembolism is considered.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AHA summary calls maternal stroke rare and life-threatening and explicitly says pregnancy should not delay evidence-based acute stroke treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A postpartum patient has seizure, severe headache and visual symptoms. Which conclusion is most appropriate for a teaching vignette?

options.text: PRES is proven from the triad alone.
The presentation requires urgent evaluation for several secondary neurologic/obstetric causes; PRES is one possibility, not a definitive diagnosis from symptoms alone.
This is necessarily primary epilepsy.
Imaging and blood pressure are irrelevant.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Published postpartum PRES cases illustrate a possible syndrome, but a case series does not make a symptom cluster diagnostic. Differential, examination, vitals, and appropriate urgent evaluation matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best characterizes the MGB Women’s Neurology Fellowship based on its public programme page?

options.text: It is a separate ABPN-certified specialty.
It is a clinical fellowship with longitudinal clinics including headache, epilepsy, stroke, MS, general and obstetrical neurology, plus electives and a variable research component.
It is a non-clinical directory category.
It guarantees certification upon completion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The MGB page explicitly describes supervised clinical experience, longitudinal clinics, two elective months and research. ABPN does not list women’s neurology as a separate certification exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: A case report describes one patient whose neurologic symptoms began after childbirth. What is the strongest valid inference?

options.text: The case establishes postpartum causality for all similar symptoms.
It provides a real published case for hypothesis-generating discussion but cannot establish population risk, causality or a universal management plan.
It replaces a guideline.
Its images may automatically be reused because the article is free to view.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Case reports document an individual experience and are not causal evidence or treatment standards. Public access does not grant reuse rights.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician is reviewing a patient with MS considering pregnancy. What is the most defensible educational step?

options.text: Apply a single relapse-rate estimate as an individual prediction.
Discuss individualized disease activity, treatment history, pregnancy goals and current drug-specific evidence with the patient and specialist team.
Stop all disease-modifying therapies without review.
Use a 2020 review as the sole current medication authority.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MS-pregnancy decisions require individualized shared planning. The linked review is foundational but dated; current product-specific sources and specialist input are necessary.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the board-status implication for this course?

options.text: There is a separate ABPN women’s neurology certification examination.
The course maps broad topics to primary ABPN neurology knowledge; women’s neurology is not listed as a separate ABPN subspecialty examination.
Course completion confers ABPN eligibility.
The MGB directory alone establishes ABPN accreditation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPN current page lists specialty and subspecialty exams, but not women’s neurology. The fellowship page does not create a board exam or certify course learners.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educator wants to place MRI images from a free-to-view pregnancy case report into course materials. What should they do?

options.text: Copy because PMC is free.
Link to the case report; verify image authenticity, de-identification and explicit reuse licence/permission before copying or embedding.
Remove the author citation and use freely.
Assume anonymization means unrestricted copyright.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view is not permission to reproduce. The programme uses links and avoids copying images or patient records; separate rights and privacy review is needed.

title: Harvard Interprofessional Palliative Care Fellowship
level: Supplementary clinical physician fellowship; the physician pathway within a distinct interprofessional programme is ACGME-accredited, but this course is independent self-study.-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Intended for physician learners who have completed core medical education; the course does not teach clinical care authority to lay learners.

The actual HIPCF physician fellowship requires prerequisite residency completion in eligible specialties; official page enumerates neurology, family medicine, internal medicine, PM&R and radiation oncology, or at least three clinical years in anesthesiology, emergency medicine, OB/GYN, psychiatry, radiology or surgery, and lists permitted residency accreditation routes. Verify current application requirements with programme.
Basic clinical reasoning, pharmacology, ethics and interprofessional teamwork.
No prerequisite or completion of this independent course creates eligibility for HIPCF, ACGME training, licensure or board examination.
objectives: Map serious-illness needs to palliative and hospice services across disease trajectories and settings.
Synthesize whole-person assessment including symptoms, function, decision-making, culture, caregiver and psychosocial/spiritual context.
Use evidence-aware symptom reasoning for pain, dyspnea, delirium and common distress without prescribing for actual patients.
Analyze benefits, burdens, uncertainty and values in treatment decisions and serious-illness communication.
Describe the contributions of interprofessional team members and build safe coordination plans.
Explain board blueprint domains and differentiate testable knowledge from observed clinical competencies.
Recognize limits of self-study, evidence currency, jurisdiction-specific law and clinical supervision.

objectives: Develop differential-first frameworks for dyspnea, nausea, constipation, fatigue, anorexia/cachexia, secretions, anxiety and delirium
identify reversible causes and emergencies
distinguish refractory symptoms from undertreated symptoms.
boardDomains: Managing suffering (40%)
emergencies/refractory symptoms (5%)
units.casePractice: produce symptom algorithm with danger signs, causes, comfort goals, escalation triggers.
units.assessment: produce symptom algorithm with danger signs, causes, comfort goals, escalation triggers.
units.prerequisites: Prior medical degree and clinical foundation are expected; this independent course is not a clinical fellowship or substitute for residency.

units.title: Communication: serious news, goals, and family meetings
objectives: Elicit understanding and information preferences
respond to emotion
share prognosis in calibrated language
elicit values
formulate and check a recommendation
facilitate family meeting with interpreter access.
boardDomains: Communication skills (2% MCQ, core observed skill)
medical interventions
units.casePractice: role-play and peer feedback
units.assessment: rubric: listen, empathy, clear information, values, plan and teach-back.
units.prerequisites: Prior medical degree and clinical foundation are expected; this independent course is not a clinical fellowship or substitute for residency.

units.title: Decision-making, ethics, law, and treatment limits
objectives: Assess decision-specific capacity
identify surrogate and advance directive
distinguish DNR from other treatment choices
reason through time-limited trials, withdrawal, conflict, conscientious objection and jurisdictional law.
boardDomains: Ethical/legal aspects (7%)
management of medical interventions (6%)
units.casePractice: create structured ethics analysis
units.assessment: rubric asks for applicable law check, patient values and proportionality.
units.prerequisites: Prior medical degree and clinical foundation are expected; this independent course is not a clinical fellowship or substitute for residency.

units.title: Hospice, home, inpatient, and care transitions
objectives: Explain U.S. Medicare hospice election/coverage rules without treating them as universal
compare home, inpatient, long-term care and consult services
prepare a safe handoff and caregiver plan
recognize limitations in access.
boardDomains: Systems/quality
management of medical interventions
prognosis
units.casePractice: design handoff and support plan
units.assessment: scored for correct caveats and contingency planning.
units.prerequisites: Prior medical degree and clinical foundation are expected; this independent course is not a clinical fellowship or substitute for residency.

units.title: Serious illness in ICU and advanced technologies
objectives: Integrate palliative goals with ICU and disease-directed treatment
conduct time-limited trial
address ventilator withdrawal, ICD deactivation, LVAD/transplant, ECMO, dialysis and surrogate conflict.
boardDomains: Medical interventions (6%)
emergencies
communication
ethics
units.casePractice: produce ethically reasoned case conference brief
units.assessment: no device/procedure instruction.
units.prerequisites: Prior medical degree and clinical foundation are expected; this independent course is not a clinical fellowship or substitute for residency.

units.title: Pediatrics, perinatal care, and developmental context
objectives: Adjust assessment and communication to developmental stage
coordinate parent/child voice and best interests
recognize pediatric/perinatal populations are specialist domains
plan bereavement support.
boardDomains: Pediatric content (about 10% blueprint)
whole-patient assessment
grief
units.casePractice: critique a public case
units.assessment: no claims of pediatric clinical competence.
units.prerequisites: Prior medical degree and clinical foundation are expected; this independent course is not a clinical fellowship or substitute for residency.

units.title: Death, grief, bereavement, and clinician resilience
objectives: Recognize signs of impending death while allowing uncertainty
explain care and after-death tasks
provide basic grief support and identify need for specialist intervention
use team reflection and self-care.
boardDomains: Impending death (3%)
grief/loss/bereavement (3%)
professionalism
units.casePractice: family information plan and reflective practice
units.assessment: rubric covers clarity, sensitivity, referral.
units.prerequisites: Prior medical degree and clinical foundation are expected; this independent course is not a clinical fellowship or substitute for residency.

units.title: Quality, equity, evidence, and interprofessional practice
objectives: Critically appraise symptom and communication evidence
identify disparities and structural barriers
apply quality-improvement tools
collaborate across disciplines and settings
distinguish practice guidance from certification competencies.
boardDomains: Interdisciplinary teamwork, quality, professionalism (2%)
quality/compliance (2%)
ethics
units.casePractice: complete small PDSA proposal using fictional aggregate data
units.assessment: score for measurement, equity and safety.
units.prerequisites: Prior medical degree and clinical foundation are expected; this independent course is not a clinical fellowship or substitute for residency.

assignment.title: Interprofessional serious-illness case portfolio (fictional vignettes only)
deliverables: Whole-person assessment, uncertainty statement and differential for symptoms
Values-aligned goals-of-care conversation plan and brief simulated transcript
Risk-aware symptom management framework with source citations and safety triggers
Hospice/setting comparison and transition handoff with current local policy check
Interprofessional team map and QI idea that includes equity and measurable outcomes

rubric.standard: Recognizes relevant symptom/differential and whole-person context; states uncertainty and information gaps.
Uses linked current primary guidance; dates guidance; distinguishes policy from guideline.
Respects decision-making, elicits values, communicates uncertainty and addresses conflict without coercive assumptions.
Names reassessment, escalation and coordination needs; no unsupervised procedural advice.
Uses team contributions appropriately and addresses access, language, caregiver and equity needs.

assignment.caseLabel: All course-authored cases are explicitly fictional; external cases are linked only.

assessment.format: Diagnostic self-test, ten original blueprint-mapped single-best-answer questions, three analytic case submissions and a communication role-play rubric.
assessment.mastery: Formative target is 80% on course questions with review of all rationales; this is not a validated predictive threshold or board-pass predictor. Communication is assessed by rubric in simulation, not by MCQs alone.
assessment.credential: No credit-bearing, accredited, continuing-medical-education, licensure, procedural, or certification outcome.

studyHours.status: Transparent independent-study plan, not a clinical-training equivalence. Suggested 120 learner hours: about 36 hours viewing a future complete original lecture series, 36 hours readings, 24 hours case/assignment work, 12 hours deliberate communication practice and 12 hours review/assessment. The video allocation is only a plan; verified ready video time currently equals zero.

unitMap.text: Foundations, scope, and concurrent care
Prognosis, illness trajectories, and uncertainty
Whole-person assessment and symptom measurement
Pain mechanisms and safe analgesic reasoning
Non-pain symptoms, emergencies, and refractory suffering
Communication: serious news, goals, and family meetings
Decision-making, ethics, law, and treatment limits
Hospice, home, inpatient, and care transitions
Serious illness in ICU and advanced technologies
Pediatrics, perinatal care, and developmental context
Death, grief, bereavement, and clinician resilience
Quality, equity, evidence, and interprofessional practice

topicGaps: The MGH and University-labelled grand-rounds playlists provide observed accessible duration above the 36-hour target (only public visible entries counted), but most recordings were not played or clinically reviewed; recordings whose titles are generic cannot be assigned topic coverage beyond the playlist designation.
A complete public internal HIPCF didactic syllabus and its proprietary lecture archive remain unavailable; the institutional rotations are supervised clinical experiences, not video hours.

Detailed, current disease-specific trajectories for heart failure, COPD, dementia, renal/liver failure, neurologic illness and pediatric/perinatal conditions remain incompletely supported by publicly titled recordings; use the board blueprint and current specialty guidance to close gaps.

Comprehensive current, patient-specific pharmacologic protocols for poly-symptom management, renal/hepatic impairment, opioid conversion/rotation, delirium and refractory symptoms are not supplied by this course or inferred from lecture titles; specialist supervision and current local protocols remain necessary.

Pediatric/perinatal assessment, developmental capacity, assent/consent, family communication and disease-specific symptom management are specialty domains; the adult physician pathway and its recordings do not establish pediatric clinical competence.

Decision-specific capacity assessment, local surrogate hierarchy, advance directive law, treatment withdrawal, assisted-dying law and hospice eligibility/coverage vary by jurisdiction and date; the course maps issues but does not provide a legal opinion or substitute local review.

Communication performance, interprofessional teamwork, professionalism, observed clinical competence, procedures, clinical supervision and actual rotations cannot be reproduced or attested by self-study videos.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: A real Hospice and Palliative Medicine subspecialty certification exam exists. The ABIM page describes the shared/cosponsored HPM certification program and states ABIM administers the exam; other board diplomates follow their own board eligibility rules. No separate current “American Board of Hospice and Palliative Medicine” exam is established by the current ABIM source. The institutional page is the programme directory, not certification authority.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Current ABIM policy states the training pathway requires 12 months of full-time clinical hospice and palliative medicine fellowship training accredited by ACGME, RCPSC or Collège des médecins du Québec, plus primary-board certification and other requirements including clinical competence, unrestricted license and passing the examination. This independent course cannot confer or substitute for any requirement. Check the chosen certifying board for current rules.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham
officialProgrammes.name: Harvard Interprofessional Palliative Care Fellowship — Physician Fellowship (physician pathway within interprofessional programme)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official overview describes one-year interprofessional clinical training and explicitly distinguishes ACGME-accredited physician fellowship from adult nurse-practitioner fellowships and ASHP-accredited PGY2 pain management/palliative-care pharmacy residency. Physician page gives rotations and prerequisites. Public pages do not supply the complete internal didactic lecture archive.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Original packet classified this as a supplementary clinical physician fellowship. Primary institutional pages verify it is genuinely a physician fellowship pathway and ACGME-accredited; this is a physician curriculum, not the NP fellowship, the PGY2 pharmacy residency, or the separate Harvard Interprofessional Pediatric Palliative Care Fellowship at Boston Children’s Hospital. The Dana-Farber page combines programme descriptions and asserts “American Board of Hospice and Palliative Medicine” accreditation; this wording conflicts with current ABIM’s account of multi-board subspecialty certification and is not relied upon for board status. Rotations described by HIPCF include inpatient consultation, inpatient palliative unit, home/general inpatient hospice, long-term care/VA, pediatric palliative care, outpatient clinic, selective, elective and vacation. Rotation schedules are actual supervised training, not video hours or an online curriculum.
sourceCaveats: No human clinical review performed. Clinical sources were reviewed on 2026-10-07; policies/guidelines can change.
The public HIPCF page establishes program structure, not the complete internal syllabus. Public source describes distinct physician, NP and pharmacy tracks.

DFCI website’s “American Board of Hospice and Palliative Medicine” wording is not used as board/certification authority. Current ABIM identifies HPM as a shared subspecialty certification and ABIM-administered exam.
The official current ABIM policy describes eligible pathways and does not mean every physician qualifies through ABIM; check own certifying board.
The current ABIM blueprint weights do not measure the overall importance of untestable observed competencies. It describes typical test content.

All external videos surfaced by search were omitted from counted hours because runtime/free access could not be observed through public metadata in this run. No estimates or duplicate entries counted.
No real patient record or clinical image has been copied. Case links have access/reuse caveats.
No treatment plan here is for an actual patient; current local guidelines and supervised clinicians govern care.

topicGaps: The MGH and University-labelled grand-rounds playlists provide observed accessible duration above the 36-hour target (only public visible entries counted), but most recordings were not played or clinically reviewed; recordings whose titles are generic cannot be assigned topic coverage beyond the playlist designation.
A complete public internal HIPCF didactic syllabus and its proprietary lecture archive remain unavailable; the institutional rotations are supervised clinical experiences, not video hours.

Detailed, current disease-specific trajectories for heart failure, COPD, dementia, renal/liver failure, neurologic illness and pediatric/perinatal conditions remain incompletely supported by publicly titled recordings; use the board blueprint and current specialty guidance to close gaps.

Comprehensive current, patient-specific pharmacologic protocols for poly-symptom management, renal/hepatic impairment, opioid conversion/rotation, delirium and refractory symptoms are not supplied by this course or inferred from lecture titles; specialist supervision and current local protocols remain necessary.

Pediatric/perinatal assessment, developmental capacity, assent/consent, family communication and disease-specific symptom management are specialty domains; the adult physician pathway and its recordings do not establish pediatric clinical competence.

Decision-specific capacity assessment, local surrogate hierarchy, advance directive law, treatment withdrawal, assisted-dying law and hospice eligibility/coverage vary by jurisdiction and date; the course maps issues but does not provide a legal opinion or substitute local review.

Communication performance, interprofessional teamwork, professionalism, observed clinical competence, procedures, clinical supervision and actual rotations cannot be reproduced or attested by self-study videos.
