practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional patient with metastatic cancer receiving active chemotherapy, what statement about palliative care is most accurate?

options.text: It can be provided concurrently with disease-directed treatment.
It requires stopping antineoplastic therapy.
It is reserved for the last days of life.
It can only be provided in hospice.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Palliative care may begin early and accompany disease-directed treatment; hospice is a distinct service/coverage pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with advanced heart failure reports episodic breathlessness. What is the best initial reasoning step?

options.text: Assess symptom experience, context, function, and potentially reversible causes before choosing a symptom plan.
Assume breathlessness means death is imminent.
Begin palliative sedation.
Discontinue heart-failure treatment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Assessment and differential diagnosis precede treatment; symptom management and disease-directed care can proceed together.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with advanced cancer and new severe pain has rising opioid exposure and new confusion. Which next step best reflects safe reasoning?

options.text: Reassess pain mechanism, cognition, medication exposure, organ function, and reversible contributors before changing therapy.
Assume all confusion is irreversible terminal delirium.
Escalate opioid immediately without reassessment.
Abruptly stop every analgesic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI pain guidance emphasizes reassessment and individualized risk; delirium and toxicity require evaluation, not a reflex dose change.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient says, “I do not want more details today.” What should the clinician do?

options.text: Respect the information preference, ask what they do want to know, and offer to revisit later.
Continue with full disclosure because all patients want maximal detail.
Ask the family to decide without the patient.
End the encounter and document refusal.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Information preferences vary. Patient-centered communication checks preference and maintains an invitation for later discussion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with decision-making capacity declines a recommended intervention. Which ethical response is most appropriate?

options.text: Explore understanding, values, and reasons; explain options and risks; respect an informed refusal while maintaining care.
Override the decision because the clinician believes it is beneficial.
Assume family preference replaces the patient’s decision.
Stop all care.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A capable patient’s informed preferences should guide choices; continue communication and appropriate care. Verify applicable local law and circumstances.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about U.S. Medicare hospice is most accurate?

options.text: It is a defined benefit with eligibility and certification rules that should be checked against current CMS policy.
Any patient receiving palliative care automatically qualifies.
Hospice always requires a six-month maximum prognosis that is certain.
Hospice is synonymous with inpatient palliative care.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hospice eligibility is policy-defined, prognosis is uncertain, and the service is not synonymous with palliative care generally.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with advanced COPD is considering a time-limited trial of noninvasive ventilation. What should the team clarify?

options.text: The patient’s goals, hoped-for benefits, burdens, duration/reassessment criteria, and what happens if the trial does not meet goals.
That all palliative patients should refuse ventilation.
That a trial is ethically invalid unless curative.
Only the family’s preference.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A time-limited trial links a treatment to patient-defined goals, observable reassessment, and contingency planning.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is most appropriate when estimating prognosis in progressive neurologic disease?

options.text: Describe trajectory and uncertainty using available evidence, then connect the discussion to decisions the patient faces.
Give an exact date of death.
Avoid prognosis entirely.
Use one prognostic score as a definitive answer.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Prognosis should be communicated transparently with uncertainty; no single estimate eliminates variability.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best captures the role of a multidisciplinary palliative team?

options.text: Coordinate complementary expertise around patient/family needs and goals with the treating clinicians.
Replace all disease-specialist care.
Limit involvement to spiritual counseling.
Require a hospice election.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Interdisciplinary collaboration and the patient/family as the unit of care are core features.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with a serious congenital condition is being considered for palliative support. Which principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Adapt symptom assessment and communication to developmental stage and family context, while attending to the child’s interests and voice.
Assume pediatric palliative care only applies after curative treatment stops.
Use adult communication techniques without adjustment.
Exclude parents from discussions in all cases.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric palliative care requires developmental and family context; adult frameworks cannot be applied without adaptation.

title: Pancreatology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (pancreas-focused subspecialty training; MGB listing is currently developmental, not an operational published curriculum)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.learnerLevel: Postgraduate physician-learner level for gastroenterology fellows/attendings; also suitable for physicians seeking structured pancreas-focused continuing study. Not an entry route to residency/fellowship.
prerequisites.required: Prior internal medicine and gastroenterology knowledge: abdominal anatomy, clinical epidemiology, interpretation of labs and cross-sectional imaging, evidence-based medicine and consent/safety principles.
prerequisites.recommended: Review ABIM GI blueprint domains 8.3–8.7, 6.7, and 10; complete acute/chronic pancreatitis and basic GI imaging fundamentals.
prerequisites.clinicalScope: Self-study only; no real-time patient care, procedural simulation/authorization or credentialing.

objectives: Synthesize pathophysiology, risk factors, clinical findings, labs, imaging and competing diagnoses in pancreatic disease.
Reason through acute pancreatitis diagnostic criteria, etiologies, severity, early care, complications and prevention using current guidance.
Evaluate chronic/recurrent pancreatitis, exocrine/endocrine dysfunction, nutrition, pain and procedural decision-making while stating uncertainty.
Interpret cystic/solid lesions, precursor risk and cancer surveillance eligibility using guideline dates and multidisciplinary referral.
Recognize autoimmune pancreatitis and key malignant/structural mimics; avoid single-test diagnostic certainty.
Appraise evidence and communicate trade-offs, access, equity and patient-centered care in pancreas disease.

units.title: Foundations: pancreas physiology, anatomy and decision tools
objectives: Map exocrine/endocrine anatomy and ductal anatomy to common syndromes.
Explain normal acinar, ductal and islet functions; distinguish disease mechanism from association.
Apply the ABIM task mix—diagnosis/testing, care decisions, prognosis, basic science—to a pancreatic presentation.
topics: Pancreas anatomy and physiology; exocrine/endocrine function; diagnostic test performance; evidence appraisal; person-centered and equitable care.
units.casePractice: Make a one-page mechanism-to-test concept map; 10-item baseline diagnostic reasoning quiz.
units.assessment: Make a one-page mechanism-to-test concept map; 10-item baseline diagnostic reasoning quiz.

units.title: Acute pancreatitis: diagnosis, causes and first assessment
objectives: Apply revised Atlanta diagnostic criteria without overcalling nonspecific enzyme/imaging findings.
Build an etiologic differential and select initial laboratory/imaging tests based on question and timing.
Recognize limitations of severity scores and reassess evolving organ failure.
topics: Characteristic pain, enzyme criteria, imaging, biliary/alcohol/metabolic/drug/iatrogenic/genetic etiologies; severity classification and complications.
units.boardDomains: 8.6; ABIM task targets Diagnosis/Testing 40%, risk/prognosis 10%, basic science 5%
units.casePractice: Interpret two fictional vignettes and state two-of-three diagnostic criteria, differential and next test; rubric: evidence, differential, test choice, uncertainty (25% each).
units.assessment: Interpret two fictional vignettes and state two-of-three diagnostic criteria, differential and next test; rubric: evidence, differential, test choice, uncertainty (25% each).

units.title: Acute pancreatitis: early care and biliary decision making
objectives: Compare current fluid strategies and identify risks of over-resuscitation.
Choose oral/enteral nutrition and antibiotic strategy consistent with current guidance.
Distinguish cholangitis/persistent obstruction from uncomplicated biliary pancreatitis when considering ERCP; plan recurrence prevention.
topics: Goal-directed fluids; early feeding; enteral vs parenteral support; antibiotics; urgent ERCP indications; cholecystectomy and etiology-specific prevention.
units.casePractice: Create an evidence-cited first-72-hour decision pathway; score 0–4 each for fluid rationale, feeding, antibiotics, ERCP, recurrence prevention.
units.assessment: Create an evidence-cited first-72-hour decision pathway; score 0–4 each for fluid rationale, feeding, antibiotics, ERCP, recurrence prevention.

units.title: Severe and necrotizing acute pancreatitis
objectives: Differentiate sterile from infected necrosis and recognize clinical deterioration/organ failure.
Sequence multidisciplinary intervention using step-up/delay principles and individual patient status.
Select time-appropriate imaging and identify when referral or escalation is needed.
topics: Collections over time; necrosis; infection assessment; ICU/supportive care; minimally invasive/endoscopic/surgical approaches; follow-up.
units.casePractice: Sequence a fictional necrotizing pancreatitis case through three time points; rubric: diagnosis, timing, source control, nutrition, team/referral (20% each).
units.assessment: Sequence a fictional necrotizing pancreatitis case through three time points; rubric: diagnosis, timing, source control, nutrition, team/referral (20% each).

units.title: Recurrent acute pancreatitis: find the cause
objectives: Structure work-up after an unrevealing initial evaluation and distinguish recurrence from chronic disease.
Select EUS/MRCP thoughtfully; assess medications, metabolic and genetic contexts.
Explain uncertain role/risks of ERCP in pancreas divisum or idiopathic recurrent AP.
topics: Recurrent acute episodes vs chronic disease; occult biliary disease; medication/metabolic/genetic and anatomic causes; EUS and MRI/MRCP selection; pancreas divisum evidence and ERCP uncertainty.
units.casePractice: Write a diagnostic plan with explicit uncertainty and harms/benefits; score 0–4 for differential, test sequencing, ERCP shared decision, follow-up.
units.assessment: Write a diagnostic plan with explicit uncertainty and harms/benefits; score 0–4 for differential, test sequencing, ERCP shared decision, follow-up.

units.title: Chronic pancreatitis and pain
objectives: Recognize chronic pancreatitis as a fibroinflammatory syndrome and evaluate by history, risk factors and cross-sectional imaging.
Address alcohol/tobacco stigma-sensitively and consider genetic/obstructive/immune/metabolic causes.
Compare endoscopic and surgical approaches for painful obstructive disease without promising benefit.
topics: Early/late disease; CT/MRI/EUS and limits; pain mechanisms; opioid-sparing multidisciplinary care; endotherapy vs surgery; AGA/ACG guidance.
units.casePractice: Compare an obstructive and a non-obstructive fictional case; rubric: mechanism, diagnostic evidence, pain/function goals, multidisciplinary shared decision.
units.assessment: Compare an obstructive and a non-obstructive fictional case; rubric: mechanism, diagnostic evidence, pain/function goals, multidisciplinary shared decision.

units.title: Chronic pancreatitis: EPI, nutrition and type 3c diabetes
objectives: Interpret fecal elastase in the proper specimen/clinical setting and avoid using imaging to diagnose EPI.
Outline PERT principles, monitoring of nutrition, micronutrients and bone health using current guidance.
Recognize diabetes secondary to pancreatic disease and coordinate individualized assessment.
topics: Steatorrhea, malnutrition, fecal elastase, PERT, nutritional assessment, fat-soluble vitamins, bone disease and pancreatogenic diabetes.
units.casePractice: Critique three fictional fecal-elastase results and draft monitoring checklist; score: specimen/context, interpretation, PERT source, nutrition follow-up.
units.assessment: Critique three fictional fecal-elastase results and draft monitoring checklist; score: specimen/context, interpretation, PERT source, nutrition follow-up.

units.title: Pancreatic cysts and precursor lesions
objectives: Classify common cystic lesions by morphology/duct relationship while avoiding certainty from one test.
Compare guideline approaches and communicate trade-offs/uncertainty in surveillance.
Identify worrisome features and multidisciplinary referral triggers.
topics: Incidental cysts; IPMN/MCN/serous lesions; MRI/MRCP, EUS-FNA indications/limits; surveillance stopping points; pathology correlation.
units.casePractice: Build a guideline comparison for two fictional cyst vignettes; rubric: source/date, risk feature, test, surveillance/shared decision (25% each).
units.assessment: Build a guideline comparison for two fictional cyst vignettes; rubric: source/date, risk feature, test, surveillance/shared decision (25% each).

units.title: Pancreatic neoplasia, screening and multidisciplinary care
objectives: Separate evaluation of a symptomatic mass from screening of asymptomatic people at inherited risk.
Interpret staging/resectability concepts and refer to multidisciplinary teams.
Explain limits/benefits of surveillance for defined high-risk groups and evidence gaps.
topics: Ductal adenocarcinoma and precursor lesions; solid/cystic malignancies; pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors; inherited-risk screening eligibility; staging/resectability concepts; multidisciplinary referrals.
units.boardDomains: 6.7, genetic cancer syndromes 6.1; ABIM neoplastic disorders; AGA high-risk screening advice
units.casePractice: Prepare a tumor-board memo for a fictional mass and a separate high-risk family-history case; score staging, risk qualification, referral, evidence.
units.assessment: Prepare a tumor-board memo for a fictional mass and a separate high-risk family-history case; score staging, risk qualification, referral, evidence.

units.title: Autoimmune pancreatitis and mimics
objectives: Compare type 1 and type 2 AIP, IgG4-related systemic disease and pancreatic malignancy mimics.
Use composite diagnostic evidence; do not diagnose from IgG4 alone or use an empiric steroid response without exclusion of cancer.
Identify extra-pancreatic clues and need for multidisciplinary expert evaluation.
topics: Type 1 IgG4-related and type 2 duct-centric AIP; serology and histology limits; imaging patterns; systemic features; cancer mimic evaluation; treatment only after diagnostic safeguards.
units.casePractice: Reason through fictional focal enlargement with jaundice; score cancer exclusion, collateral evidence, serology limitation, safe next step.
units.assessment: Reason through fictional focal enlargement with jaundice; score cancer exclusion, collateral evidence, serology limitation, safe next step.

units.title: Pancreatic fluid collections, duct disorders and procedures
objectives: Classify fluid collections by morphology/timing and identify nonprocedural vs intervention questions.
Compare EUS, MRCP, ERCP and interventional options at conceptual level.
Describe procedural risks/alternatives, consent and referral boundaries; no hands-on competence claim.
topics: Revised Atlanta collection nomenclature and timing; pseudocyst vs acute necrotic collection vs walled-off necrosis; disconnected duct syndrome; EUS/MRCP/ERCP indications, risk and referral.
units.casePractice: Create an imaging-to-management decision tree; rubric: nomenclature, indication, alternatives/risks, referral, follow-up (20% each).
units.assessment: Create an imaging-to-management decision tree; rubric: nomenclature, indication, alternatives/risks, referral, follow-up (20% each).

units.title: Research, quality, communication and synthesis
objectives: Critically appraise a pancreatitis trial/guideline and distinguish evidence from expert consensus.
Present an accessible, culturally responsive shared-decision conversation and minimize stigma.
Integrate the pancreas differential in a timed, case-based board-style assessment.
topics: Trial design and bias; outcomes meaningful to patients; guideline strength/limits; shared decision-making; stigma and disparities; patient safety, QI and evidence communication.
units.boardDomains: All ABIM task domains; ACGME competencies and patient safety
units.casePractice: Capstone oral case conference and evidence brief; pass criterion ≥80% rubric score is course practice only, not board prediction or clinical credential.
units.assessment: Capstone oral case conference and evidence brief; pass criterion ≥80% rubric score is course practice only, not board prediction or clinical credential.

assignment.name: Pancreatology clinical reasoning portfolio (fictional cases only)
components: Two acute pancreatitis diagnostic/management plans; one severe/necrotizing case; one recurrent unexplained case.
One chronic pancreatitis/EPI/nutrition case with specimen/test limitations.
One pancreatic cyst guideline comparison and one cancer-risk eligibility memo.
One AIP-vs-malignancy differential and a 1,000-word evidence appraisal of one guideline/trial.
Ten original multiple-choice questions below plus a reflective note on uncertainty and scope.

rubric.criterion: Communication, uncertainty, equity and scope boundaries

assignment.passThreshold: Practice threshold ≥80% portfolio rubric only; not a validated examination predictor, board exam, clinical credential or pass guarantee. Faculty review is recommended before use.

assessment.formative: Self-check at every unit; 10 original MCQs with answer/rationales; learner labels evidence certainty.
assessment.summative: Portfolio/rubric and timed capstone case; ≥80% internal course target only, no validated psychometrics or board prediction.
assessment.integrity: Questions are original educational items, not official or recalled/proprietary board items. Cases are expressly fictional.
assessment.safety: No assessment authorizes diagnosis/treatment or procedures for actual patients.

studyHours.plan: A 12-week self-study plan at ~7.5 hours/week (90 hours total): 30 hours verified open external lectures, 24 hours guideline/textbook reading, 24 hours cases/assignments, 12 hours review/questions. This is a transparent learner study plan, not clinical training hours; the current ready video ledger contains 11.54 hours, so substitute planned media with readings until future films are genuinely recorded and checked.
studyHours.hoursPlanNotClaim: Planned lecture production is not counted as completed/ready media.

unitMap.text: Foundations: pancreas physiology, anatomy and decision tools
coveredTopics: Pancreas anatomy and physiology; exocrine/endocrine function; diagnostic test performance; evidence appraisal; person-centered and equitable care.

unitMap.text: Acute pancreatitis: diagnosis, causes and first assessment
coveredTopics: Characteristic pain, enzyme criteria, imaging, biliary/alcohol/metabolic/drug/iatrogenic/genetic etiologies; severity classification and complications.

unitMap.text: Acute pancreatitis: early care and biliary decision making
coveredTopics: Goal-directed fluids; early feeding; enteral vs parenteral support; antibiotics; urgent ERCP indications; cholecystectomy and etiology-specific prevention.

unitMap.text: Severe and necrotizing acute pancreatitis
coveredTopics: Collections over time; necrosis; infection assessment; ICU/supportive care; minimally invasive/endoscopic/surgical approaches; follow-up.

unitMap.text: Recurrent acute pancreatitis: find the cause
coveredTopics: Recurrent acute episodes vs chronic disease; occult biliary disease; medication/metabolic/genetic and anatomic causes; EUS and MRI/MRCP selection; pancreas divisum evidence and ERCP uncertainty.

unitMap.text: Chronic pancreatitis and pain
coveredTopics: Early/late disease; CT/MRI/EUS and limits; pain mechanisms; opioid-sparing multidisciplinary care; endotherapy vs surgery; AGA/ACG guidance.

unitMap.text: Chronic pancreatitis: EPI, nutrition and type 3c diabetes
coveredTopics: Steatorrhea, malnutrition, fecal elastase, PERT, nutritional assessment, fat-soluble vitamins, bone disease and pancreatogenic diabetes.

unitMap.text: Pancreatic cysts and precursor lesions
coveredTopics: Incidental cysts; IPMN/MCN/serous lesions; MRI/MRCP, EUS-FNA indications/limits; surveillance stopping points; pathology correlation.

unitMap.text: Pancreatic neoplasia, screening and multidisciplinary care
coveredTopics: Ductal adenocarcinoma and precursor lesions; solid/cystic malignancies; pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors; inherited-risk screening eligibility; staging/resectability concepts; multidisciplinary referrals.

unitMap.text: Autoimmune pancreatitis and mimics
coveredTopics: Type 1 IgG4-related and type 2 duct-centric AIP; serology and histology limits; imaging patterns; systemic features; cancer mimic evaluation; treatment only after diagnostic safeguards.

unitMap.text: Pancreatic fluid collections, duct disorders and procedures
coveredTopics: Revised Atlanta collection nomenclature and timing; pseudocyst vs acute necrotic collection vs walled-off necrosis; disconnected duct syndrome; EUS/MRCP/ERCP indications, risk and referral.

unitMap.text: Research, quality, communication and synthesis

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A patient has characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back and serum lipase >3 times the upper reference limit. CT is not yet available. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis is established by two of three accepted criteria.
CT is mandatory before diagnosis.
Lipase alone establishes the diagnosis in every setting.
A normal ultrasound excludes pancreatitis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Two of three criteria suffice: characteristic pain, enzyme elevation at least three times upper limit, or characteristic imaging. Avoid routine early CT when diagnosis is clear; interpret tests in context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: In a patient with acute biliary pancreatitis, there is no cholangitis and no evidence of persistent common-duct obstruction. Which statement best reflects guideline-based approach?

options.text: Urgent ERCP is routine for all biliary pancreatitis.
Urgent ERCP is not routine absent cholangitis/ongoing obstruction; reassess and use appropriate biliary evaluation.
Prophylactic antibiotics prevent pancreatic necrosis.
Keep nil per os until lipase normalizes.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2024 ACG guideline and AGA guidance discourage routine early ERCP without cholangitis/ongoing obstruction. Antibiotics and prolonged fasting are not routine pancreatitis interventions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A hemodynamically stable patient has severe necrotizing pancreatitis without evidence of infection. Which general principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Immediate open necrosectomy for every necrotic collection.
Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics until imaging normalizes.
Supportive care and multidisciplinary, usually delayed/step-up intervention only for a clinical indication.
Routine ERCP to drain sterile necrosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Necrosis alone is not an indication for prophylactic antibiotics or immediate open debridement. Delayed, minimally invasive step-up approaches are generally preferred when intervention is needed, with individualized multidisciplinary decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A patient with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhea and weight loss. Which test is the preferred initial test for EPI per AGA update?

options.text: Pancreatic CT to measure enzyme output.
Fecal elastase on semi-solid or solid stool.
Response to empiric PERT alone.
Serum lipase during a pain-free interval.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AGA identifies fecal elastase as the most appropriate initial test, on semi-solid or solid stool; watery stool can dilute it. Imaging cannot diagnose EPI, and response to a therapeutic trial is unreliable as a diagnostic test.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: Fecal elastase is 150 μg/g in a watery stool sample. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Definite EPI; begin treatment without context.
Indeterminate result; watery specimen may falsely lower concentration, so repeat/interpret in clinical context.
Pancreatic cancer is proven.
Normal exocrine function is confirmed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AGA update describes 100–200 μg/g as indeterminate and requires semi-solid/solid stool. The assay is interpreted with clinical context; this result does not diagnose a cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: After a negative initial evaluation for recurrent acute pancreatitis, which test does AGA expert advice prefer for further diagnostic evaluation?

options.text: Endoscopic ultrasound; MRI/MRCP is a reasonable complementary or alternative test based on expertise/availability.
Diagnostic ERCP for everyone.
Repeat serum lipase monthly.
Routine pancreatic biopsy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AGA advises EUS after unrevealing initial evaluation; contrast MRI with cholangiopancreatography is a reasonable complement or alternative. ERCP has uncertain benefit and potentially severe adverse events in unexplained recurrence.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A patient with pancreas divisum has recurrent pancreatitis but no objective evidence of dorsal duct obstruction. Which statement about ERCP is best?

options.text: ERCP is proven to prevent recurrence and should be automatic.
ERCP has no role for pain alone; role in recurrence reduction is controversial and requires careful individualized discussion.
Pancreas divisum proves the cause of every episode.
Dual sphincterotomy is mandatory.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AGA notes the role of ERCP in pancreas divisum is controversial; minor-papilla therapy may be considered especially with objective outflow obstruction, but no ERCP for pain alone. Risk/uncertain benefit should be discussed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A 2-cm asymptomatic pancreatic cyst has no solid component or duct dilation on imaging. Which is the best initial learning point?

options.text: No follow-up is ever needed.
Use a current guideline, incorporate surgical candidacy/preferences and discuss surveillance risks/benefits; guideline approaches differ.
Proceed directly to pancreatectomy.
A cyst fluid test is required for every cyst.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Cyst guidance is conditional and approaches differ across societies; AGA’s 2015 recommendations are older and should be compared with updated specialty guidance. Discuss the rationale and patient context, not a one-size-fits-all intervention.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A high-risk asymptomatic individual asks about pancreatic cancer screening. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Screen all adults with annual CT.
Screening decisions are limited to selected inherited/familial high-risk groups and should follow expert-center guidance; not population-wide.
CA 19-9 alone is a screening test.
A first-degree relative with no other risk always guarantees screening eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guidance targets defined high-risk individuals; do not generalize to population screening or assume all family histories meet criteria. Eligibility and preferred modality depend on current guidance and patient/family context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A focal pancreatic enlargement has elevated serum IgG4. What is the safest reasoning?

options.text: IgG4 elevation alone proves autoimmune pancreatitis and excludes cancer.
Use composite diagnostic criteria and evaluate malignancy; IgG4 alone is not definitive.
Give a steroid trial before any cancer evaluation.
Type 1 and type 2 AIP are identical disorders.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IgG4 is one datum; the differential includes pancreatic cancer. AIP evaluation uses clinical, imaging, serologic, histologic and other-organ evidence as applicable. Steroids should not substitute for a safe malignancy evaluation.

Interpret MRI, CSF and AQP4/MOG antibody tests in clinical context.
Differentiate MS, MOGAD, AQP4-NMOSD, ADEM and important mimics.
Summarize evidence, current FDA label boundaries and longitudinal multidisciplinary issues.
Critically appraise evidence and communicate uncertainty in age-appropriate terms.

units.title: 1. Pediatric neuroimmunology: approach, phenotype and localization

units.title: 2. Acquired demyelinating syndromes in childhood
objectives: Classify ADEM, CIS, MS, NMOSD and MOGAD with age-appropriate criteria and longitudinal context.

units.title: 3. Pediatric MS diagnostics and misdiagnosis avoidance
objectives: Apply current diagnostic framework alongside pediatric-specific context and exclusion of better explanations.

boardDomains: ABPN child neurology: demyelinating diseases (5–7% blueprint category)

units.title: 4. MRI pattern recognition and radiology-clinical integration
objectives: Describe brain/orbit/spinal lesion distribution without treating any single sign as pathognomonic.

topicGaps: Observed-duration, free public recordings total 4.046944 unique hours; the 36-hour floor remains short by 31.953056 hours. Newly surfaced pediatric lectures had no inspectable player duration in this run and remain excluded.
Full, pediatric-focused MRI case conference instruction with authentic lawful case access and expert image review remains insufficient; no diagnostic images were copied or independently interpreted.

Detailed pediatric treatment comparisons across MS, MOGAD and AQP4-NMOSD, including up-to-date label/off-label boundaries and longitudinal safety evidence, remain incomplete; the 2025 fingolimod label is not a complete treatment guideline.
Pediatric MOG-IgG/AQP4-IgG assay performance, low-pretest false positives, timing, discordant results and rare seronegative NMOSD require additional case-based instruction and specialist review.

Recent 2024 McDonald criteria (published 2025) have only abstract-level accessible article evidence in this packet; child-specific validation/application limits require full-text review and expert interpretation.
Cognition, fatigue, school accommodations, transition, family-centered communication, rare-disease trial design and pediatric research ethics need further teaching beyond the linked open reviews.

NMOSD Part II treatment recommendations were not readable in the original research inspection because of an access challenge; avoid expanding treatment particulars from that source without verification.
No qualified human clinician reviewed this expanded packet; the written episodes are not clinical education credentialing or treatment direction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 13-year-old has acute encephalopathy with multifocal T2 lesions after a febrile illness. Which statement is best?

options.text: This is diagnostic of MS because lesions are multifocal.
ADEM is a key syndrome-level consideration; distinguish encephalopathy and evaluate mimics before assigning etiology.
MOGAD is proven by age alone.
A normal AQP4 assay proves MS.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Encephalopathy with multifocal lesions in a child should prompt ADEM among alternatives, but neither MRI distribution nor age alone proves etiology; evaluate clinically and longitudinally.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adolescent has a first optic neuritis event and nonspecific periventricular T2 foci. What is the most defensible next step?

options.text: Diagnose MS from MRI alone.
Apply diagnostic criteria with careful clinical/MRI review and assess alternatives; do not infer MS from nonspecific lesions alone.
Start long-term DMT without a diagnosis.
Repeat MOG antibody testing monthly regardless of phenotype.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Criteria require a compatible syndrome and sufficient evidence with no better explanation; pediatric mimics and nonspecific lesions are important.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which test is preferred in suspected AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD per NEMOS recommendations?

options.text: Serum AQP4-IgG using a cell-based assay.
CSF-only AQP4 ELISA.
Serum MOG-IgG as the sole NMOSD test.
AQP4 imaging biomarker.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NEMOS recommends standardized cell-based assays for AQP4-IgG and emphasizes phenotype, MRI and differential evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is a necessary conceptual safeguard when interpreting a positive MOG-IgG result?

options.text: Any positive result establishes MOGAD irrespective of phenotype.
Interpret within a compatible core clinical event, assay context, and differential/pretest probability.
A positive result excludes all other CNS diseases.
MOG-IgG is interchangeable with AQP4-IgG.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The international criteria are clinical-serologic constructs; serology alone is not a diagnosis and testing in low-pretest contexts may mislead.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with new neurologic deficit has fever and a urinary infection. Before labeling an MS relapse, what is the best reasoning?

options.text: Assume new inflammatory activity.
Assess for infection/other pseudo-relapse triggers and localize/characterize the deficit; urgent evaluation may be needed.
Stop all medication immediately.
Use MRI enhancement alone to classify symptoms.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Intercurrent illness may worsen old symptoms; evaluate new deficits and triggers rather than assuming relapse. This is an educational reasoning principle, not a treatment order.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which current FDA label statement is accurate for fingolimod?

options.text: FDA indication begins at age 2 for all demyelinating disease.
It is indicated for relapsing forms of MS including CIS, RRMS and active SPMS in patients 10 years and older; initiation monitoring and contraindications matter.
FDA indication covers AQP4-NMOSD.
It is a rescue treatment for acute myelitis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 label states the indication for relapsing MS from age 10 and has detailed pre-start evaluation, first-dose monitoring, warnings and contraindications.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which item describes the MGB program's current official catalogue designation?

options.text: ACGME-accredited subspecialty board pathway.
Non-GME fellowship listing in MGB's current GME catalogue; older directory uses legacy 'GME accredited by Partners' wording.
Research-only postdoc with no patient-care exposure.
UCNS-certified pediatric MS program.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current MGB catalogue labels the fellowship Non-GME while the older page says GME accredited by Partners; resolve with institution and do not equate either with ACGME accreditation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which examination directly maps to this course's board-cognitive objectives?

options.text: Separate ABMS Pediatric MS board exam.
ABPN Neurology with Special Qualification in Child Neurology content blueprint includes demyelinating diseases and neuroimmunologic disorders; no separate pediatric MS examination is listed.
UCNS pediatric neuroimmunology exam.
A course completion test confers board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPN blueprint lists demyelinating diseases and neuroimmunologic/paraneoplastic disorders; ABMS and UCNS current lists do not show a separate pediatric MS/neuroimmunology board examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: A spinal cord lesion extends over several vertebral segments in a child with optic neuritis. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: It establishes NMOSD.
It is a pattern prompting careful differential including AQP4-NMOSD and MOGAD; integrate antibodies, MRI, clinical syndrome and criteria.
It excludes all inflammatory disease.
It is pathognomonic for MS.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Longitudinally extensive myelitis is a differential clue, not a stand-alone diagnosis; NEMOS emphasizes serum antibody testing and exclusion of mimics.

practiceQuestions.stem: A family asks whether this independent course certifies a trainee in neuroimmunology. Best response?

options.text: Yes, if they pass the quiz.
No. It is independent self-study, not accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence or certification.
It grants ABPN child neurology certification.
It substitutes for supervised clinic time.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Course completion has no credentialing authority and cannot replace formal training or supervised experience.

title: Intraoperative Neurophysiology Monitoring Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (non-ACGME IONM fellowship; educational track is distinct from ACGME Clinical Neurophysiology fellowship)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Completion of US ACGME-accredited Neurology residency for actual institutional applicant context; this course itself does not certify eligibility.
Foundational neuroanatomy, neurophysiology, EEG/EMG and evoked-potential concepts; basic perioperative team and anesthesia vocabulary.
Learner should be a supervised physician trainee or other appropriately qualified adult learner; public self-study does not confer clinical privileges.
objectives: Design a question-led educational monitoring plan from procedure, anatomy, risks and available baseline information.
Explain SSEP, transcranial electrical MEP, EMG, EEG, BAEP/VEP and mapping principles and limitations.
Interpret evolving signals against technical acquisition, anesthesia, systemic physiology, positioning and surgical timing without overclaiming.
Communicate a signal change promptly, clearly and with calibrated uncertainty to an interprofessional team.
Appraise evidence for prediction, false negatives, case selection and limits of intervention claims.
Differentiate official institution training, ACGME CNP accreditation, ABPN Clinical Neurophysiology subspecialty certification and ABNM IONM credential.

unitMap.text: Evidence appraisal, integration and capstone

topicGaps: The 36-hour recorded-video floor is unmet: 1.9836 verified external hours across three unique free public recordings, leaving 34.0164 hours. Planned scripts and originalClipPlan target minutes are not rendered or countable hours.

External coverage is concentrated in general IONM/spinal monitoring, SSEP/MEP, anesthetic influences, and alert troubleshooting. Recordings are supplementary lectures rather than a validated or complete course.
Unit 5 remains thin: detailed free-run/triggered EMG interpretation, cranial nerve-specific monitoring, and BAEP/VEP limitations lack verified long-form recorded coverage.
Unit 9 remains thin: posterior-fossa/skull-base and cranial-nerve applications are not substantively taught by the verified recordings.
Unit 10 remains thin: awake/anesthetized functional mapping, language and epilepsy workflows, afterdischarges, and patient/task prerequisites lack verified recorded coverage.
Unit 11 remains thin: supervision and role boundaries, remote-service safeguards, privacy, documentation, and quality review lack verified recorded coverage.
Unit 12 has a short evidence-appraisal chapter but lacks in-depth recording coverage of study design, serial-alert outcomes, intervention-effect evidence, and capstone integration.
Source gaps remain in public runtime-verifiable recordings for these domains. Source reading and authored scripts do not replace the missing recorded hours.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (non-ACGME IONM fellowship; educational track is distinct from ACGME Clinical Neurophysiology fellowship)
boardNames: ABPN subspecialty certification examination in Clinical Neurophysiology (not IONM-specific)
ABNM Certification Examination in Neurophysiologic Monitoring, Part I written and Part II oral (professional IONM credential; not physician specialty-board certification)
medical.boardStatus: No separate ABPN physician specialty/subspecialty board examination specifically in IONM was identified. ABPN offers an adjacent subspecialty certification examination in Clinical Neurophysiology, but current published eligibility requires primary Neurology or Child Neurology certification and one year of ACGME-accredited Clinical Neurophysiology fellowship training; this MGB IONM fellowship is explicitly non-ACGME and is not represented as satisfying that requirement. ABNM separately offers written and oral professional IONM certification examinations, open to specified doctoral backgrounds and not limited to physicians; its experience/case prerequisites are independent. Verify all current terms directly with each board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Institutional eligibility is not equivalent to ABPN board eligibility. Official MGB pages differ slightly in phrasing: the older Neurology listing says board-eligible Neurology; GME page says board-certified or board-eligible Neurology, completed ACGME US Neurology residency, and Massachusetts licensure eligibility. Neither listing promises IONM board certification or guarantees eligibility for ABPN Clinical Neurophysiology certification. ABNM candidacy has separate published education, coursework, case-log, experience and supervision requirements.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham
officialProgrammes.name: MGB Intraoperative Neurophysiology Monitoring and Mapping Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Institutional directory describes a stand-alone one-year fellowship: 2 months theory/workshops/OR setup; 6 months OR monitoring and mapping; 4 months OR plus non-OR, case prioritization, technologist supervision under attending guidance and research. It asks candidates to be board-eligible in Neurology and have completed residency in good standing; older directory wording.

officialProgrammes.institution: Massachusetts General Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: MGH Intraoperative Neurophysiology Monitoring Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: MGB GME profile calls it a one-year non-ACGME fellowship. It states applicants must complete US Neurology residency and be eligible for Massachusetts licensure, with prior CNP/epilepsy/EEG experience recommended; its application section states board-certified or board-eligible Neurology and ACGME-accredited US residency. The institution is the same fellowship variant, kept as a separate official institutional listing.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Two official URLs in supplied exact packet represent the same MGB/MGH one-year clinical physician IONM fellowship, not two curricula. The MGB GME page explicitly labels it non-GME/non-ACGME. This is an institutional program listing, not evidence of accreditation, independent board specialty status, exam eligibility, or complete public lecture curriculum. Classification decision: this is an actual physician clinical fellowship offered at the named institutions, but not a separate ACGME-accredited physician specialty or an IONM-specific board specialty; it is not a combined residency/fellowship programme, not a generic directory category, and not a research-only appointment or non-physician supplement.
sourceCaveats: Institutional sites both identify a one-year fellowship; current GME listing explicitly says non-ACGME, superseding any assumption that it is an accredited standalone IONM track.

The MGH and MGB Neurology listings preserve separate official variant labels/URLs, though they describe one system fellowship. Minor published eligibility phrasing differs and should be checked with programme administrators.

ABPN Clinical Neurophysiology is a real adjacent physician subspecialty board examination, not a board in IONM. ACGME standards describe broader Clinical Neurophysiology and include IONM among competencies/experiences. Current ABPN page requires an ACGME-accredited CNP fellowship year; MGB IONM is non-ACGME.

ABNM offers a separate written/oral IONM professional credential exam and publishes eligibility across certain science and allied-health doctoral degrees. It is not equivalent to ABPN physician specialty certification.

At least three public recordings were discovered by search, but direct duration/player metadata was not verifiable using allowed stateless tools. All remain excluded. No private/login-only footage was accessed.
Clinical review by a qualified physician has not been performed.

Track classification: actual clinical physician fellowship at MGB/MGH; one non-ACGME institutional fellowship, not a combined programme or separate board specialty, and not a non-physician/research-only directory supplement.

topicGaps: The 36-hour recorded-video floor is unmet: 1.9836 verified external hours across three unique free public recordings, leaving 34.0164 hours. Planned scripts and originalClipPlan target minutes are not rendered or countable hours.

External coverage is concentrated in general IONM/spinal monitoring, SSEP/MEP, anesthetic influences, and alert troubleshooting. Recordings are supplementary lectures rather than a validated or complete course.
Unit 5 remains thin: detailed free-run/triggered EMG interpretation, cranial nerve-specific monitoring, and BAEP/VEP limitations lack verified long-form recorded coverage.
Unit 9 remains thin: posterior-fossa/skull-base and cranial-nerve applications are not substantively taught by the verified recordings.
Unit 10 remains thin: awake/anesthetized functional mapping, language and epilepsy workflows, afterdischarges, and patient/task prerequisites lack verified recorded coverage.
Unit 11 remains thin: supervision and role boundaries, remote-service safeguards, privacy, documentation, and quality review lack verified recorded coverage.
Unit 12 has a short evidence-appraisal chapter but lacks in-depth recording coverage of study design, serial-alert outcomes, intervention-effect evidence, and capstone integration.
Source gaps remain in public runtime-verifiable recordings for these domains. Source reading and authored scripts do not replace the missing recorded hours.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best expresses the primary clinical purpose of IONM?

options.text: To guarantee no postoperative neurologic deficit
To detect significant signal change, investigate likely cause and localize risk in time to inform the operative team
To replace postoperative neurologic examination
To independently direct surgical actions

practiceQuestions.rationale: IONM provides time-sensitive neurophysiological information to the team. It cannot guarantee prevention, diagnose every mechanism, or replace clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a high-risk spinal procedure, which modality combination can provide complementary information on sensory and motor pathways?

options.text: SSEP and transcranial electrical MEP
EEG alone
BAEP alone
Triggered EMG alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAN/ACNS guidance addresses SSEP and transcranial electrical MEP together as complementary approaches; this is not a claim they are interchangeable or perfect.

practiceQuestions.stem: A sustained, important evoked-potential change occurs during spinal surgery. What is the best immediate communication principle?

options.text: Wait until closure to mention it
Promptly alert the surgical/anesthesia team that risk is increased, describe the change and support structured evaluation
Conclude permanent injury has occurred
Continue averaging without notifying anyone

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guideline recommendation is to alert the surgical team about increased risk when important IOM changes occur; inference must remain calibrated.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about a normal IONM trace is most accurate?

options.text: It excludes all later neurologic deficits
It rules out delayed injury
It reduces concern but cannot guarantee absence of injury; false negatives and delayed deficits are possible
It proves the nerves are anatomically intact

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAN/ACNS guideline notes false-negative monitoring and that neither method predicts deficits arising hours or days later.

practiceQuestions.stem: A muscle MEP becomes difficult to elicit after anesthetic change and neuromuscular blocking medication. Which first step is most appropriate?

options.text: Assume corticospinal injury
Review anesthetic/NMBA changes and technical/stimulation factors with anesthesia while checking other modalities and physiology
Increase stimulus indefinitely without consultation
Ignore the change if SSEPs persist

practiceQuestions.rationale: Muscle MEPs are sensitive to anesthetic and neuromuscular blockade effects. A differential and coordinated review are required before attributing loss to neural injury.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which interpretation is most appropriate for a unilateral SSEP loss with preserved MEPs in a fictional spinal case?

options.text: It proves technical artifact
It proves a central stroke
It is a meaningful change that needs prompt communication and systematic technical, physiologic, anesthetic and surgical differential; modalities need not move together
It can be ignored because MEPs remain

practiceQuestions.rationale: Different modalities may change independently; one-sided SSEP loss can have technical, systemic or central causes and must be escalated, not overdiagnosed.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is a key reason to obtain reproducible baselines before critical surgical maneuvers?

options.text: They establish comparators and reveal whether the signal is trackable under current technical and physiologic conditions
They guarantee every later waveform will be interpretable
They permit use of a universal percentage threshold in all cases
They replace review of preoperative neurologic status

practiceQuestions.rationale: Baselines anchor longitudinal interpretation and help identify technical limitations; they do not establish universal thresholds or guarantee subsequent interpretability.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which official statement about the MGH/MGB IONM fellowship is accurate?

options.text: It is an ACGME-accredited IONM specialty board program
The MGB GME page explicitly labels it non-ACGME and describes a one-year physician fellowship
It is a technologist-only program
Completion alone confers ABPN Clinical Neurophysiology certification

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current MGB listing labels it a non-ACGME fellowship; ABPN CNP certification requires an ACGME-accredited CNP fellowship year plus primary Neurology/Child Neurology certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which credential distinction is correct?

options.text: ABNM is only a physician board certificate
ABNM accepts specified doctoral-level backgrounds and has separate written/oral exams; it is not an ACGME physician specialty certification
ABPN provides a board in intraoperative monitoring specifically
Any IONM fellowship completion confers ABNM eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABNM describes doctoral-level science/clinical allied health pathways and case/experience requirements; PTC lists written and oral examinations. This is different from ABPN subspecialty certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a simulated mapping plan, language mapping is to be considered for a patient with a lesion near presumed dominant-hemisphere language cortex. What is a relevant preoperative planning step?

options.text: Establish an appropriate baseline language examination/task with the clinical team and plan mapping with supervising experts
Assume handedness establishes exact language dominance
Treat a single stimulation response as a validated diagnosis
Skip task comprehension checks

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official MGH curriculum describes preoperative language testing for baseline and epilepsy mapping planning; actual mapping requires supervised clinical competence and case-specific judgment.

medical.boardStatus: Actual one-year MGB physician fellowship and practice focus; not an ABPN/ABMS-recognized neurohospitalist subspecialty examination category. ABPN adult neurology is the adjacent underlying primary board. NHS core-competency authors expressly did not intend their framework as a path to neurohospitalist board certification. MGB page does not state this individual fellowship’s accreditation status.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: MGB programme page says entrants completed an ACGME-accredited adult neurology residency and have ABPN adult neurology board-eligible/board-certified status, typically entering at PGY-5. ABPN eligibility depends on its current qualifying training, licensure and application rules. This course gives no eligibility/training credit.

practiceQuestions.stem: Abrupt disabling deficits; CT excludes hemorrhage; potential IVT window remains. What process principle?

options.text: Wait for advanced perfusion in every case
If clinically eligible, treat as rapidly and safely as possible; avoid unnecessary imaging delay
Low NIHSS excludes disabling stroke
Delay vascular imaging for creatinine in every case

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current AHA/ASA guidance emphasizes rapid eligible IVT and avoiding delays for multimodal imaging not needed for that decision; treating team assesses eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: Patient remains unresponsive after convulsions stop. Which test can detect occult ongoing ictal activity?

options.text: Routine nerve conduction study
Continuous EEG when indicated/available with expert interpretation
NIHSS repeated instead of EEG
No testing because movements stopped

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACNS consensus describes cEEG use in critically ill patients with persistent unexplained impaired consciousness/seizure concern.

practiceQuestions.stem: Several minutes of continuing convulsive activity without recovery. Best organizing principle?

options.text: Wait 30 minutes
Treat as time-critical status: stabilize, address reversible causes, initiate acute treatment and escalate as needed
Outpatient EEG first
Assume epilepsy; omit etiologic evaluation

practiceQuestions.rationale: 2025 hospital guidance uses ≥5 minutes as the status operational definition, emphasizes early intervention and investigation; it is UK-context guidance with a correction notice.

practiceQuestions.stem: Before BD/DNC determination, which concern must be resolved?

options.text: Family agreement alone is physiologic prerequisite
Drug/intoxicant confounding and other prerequisites under applicable guideline/policy
CT alone establishes BD/DNC
Poor prognosis equals BD/DNC

practiceQuestions.rationale: 2023 multisociety guidance requires known catastrophic permanent injury and prerequisites/confounder exclusion; BD/DNC is not prognosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fever, subacute behavior change, new seizure; encephalitis possible. Best response?

options.text: Wait all CSF results before discussing treatment
Coordinate urgent investigation and timely empiric care with specialist/local protocols; do not use archived guideline as only current authority
Temporal MRI signal proves etiology
Assume autoimmune disease

practiceQuestions.rationale: IDSA page labels its 2008 guideline archived; urgent encephalitis reasoning must integrate tests and current local guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: LP requested in a deteriorating patient with focal signs. Best response?

options.text: Always do LP before imaging
Review indication and patient-specific safety; obtain imaging/review as appropriate and defer if unresolved risk
Never do LP in any focal deficit
Case-page diagnosis authorizes LP

practiceQuestions.rationale: Procedure timing depends on indication and patient-specific safety assessment; the linked consensus is a resource but specific advice was not extracted in this pass.

practiceQuestions.stem: Teaching MRI shows diffusion restriction after seizure. Most defensible reading?

options.text: Always arterial infarct
Peri-ictal change can mimic/coexist with vascular/inflammatory disease; integrate distribution, chronology, EEG and clinical context
Image proves epilepsy only
Seizures never affect MRI

practiceQuestions.rationale: Postictal signal changes vary; no image alone is diagnostic ground truth. NHS framework calls for clinical interpretation of ancillary studies.

practiceQuestions.stem: QI project shortens door-to-CT but tracks no outcome or complications. Main issue?

options.text: Process speed proves benefit
Add valid outcome and balancing measures; process improvement is not itself a patient outcome
Avoid equity analysis
Proves board value

practiceQuestions.rationale: NHS framework includes QI; ABPN exam blueprint includes systems-based practice. Process metrics cannot alone establish benefit/safety.

practiceQuestions.stem: Severe sudden headache and focal signs; initial CT normal. Best reasoning?

options.text: Close because normal CT excludes all secondary causes
Reassess timing/syndrome and consider vascular, infectious, pressure causes; select next tests with urgent input
Migraine by severity alone
One bedside sign excludes posterior circulation disease

practiceQuestions.rationale: A normal initial scan has pathology- and timing-dependent limitations; acute headache and vascular domains require continued clinical reasoning.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does a high score on this independent course permit?

options.text: Separate neurohospitalist board eligibility
Independent practice/procedure competence
Formative feedback only; no affiliation, accredited training, licensure, eligibility or competence
Guaranteed ABPN pass

practiceQuestions.rationale: MGB fellowship is distinct from this independent course; NHS competencies were not designed as board pathway and ABPN requires qualifying training/licensure.

title: Advanced Hepatology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional advanced-hepatology label; transplant-hepatology clinical focus)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced post-GI fellowship self-study for physicians and supervised clinical learners; not a substitute for postgraduate medical training.
required: Foundational internal medicine and gastroenterology knowledge
Basic abdominal imaging and pathology literacy
Familiarity with evidence appraisal, clinical probability and medication safety
recommended: Prior accredited gastroenterology training for learners following the standard transplant-hepatology pathway
Basic understanding of immunology, pharmacology and transplant systems
prerequisites.limits: Independent self-study does not confer admission to fellowship, supervised patient-care privileges, competence to perform procedures, licensure, credentialing or board eligibility.

objectives: Synthesize clinical, biochemical, imaging and pathology data to structure advanced liver-disease differentials and identify time-critical decompensation.

Apply current authoritative guidance to discuss complications of cirrhosis, acute liver failure, chronic liver diseases and liver malignancy, while recognizing individual contraindications and uncertainty.
Reason through transplant referral, candidate/donor evaluation, perioperative risk, allograft dysfunction, rejection, infection and immunosuppressant interactions at a board-blueprint level.
Interpret the ABIM transplant-hepatology blueprint's task and content categories and connect questions to diagnosis/testing, care decisions, prognosis and basic science.
Use ethical, patient-centered, equitable and evidence-aware reasoning, and distinguish educational case discussion from patient-specific recommendations.

units.title: Advanced liver assessment, severity and diagnostic reasoning
objectives: Classify hepatocellular, cholestatic and mixed biochemical patterns and prioritize urgent causes.
Use synthetic function, clinical context and longitudinal trends without treating a score as a diagnosis.
Build a focused differential across chronic injury, vascular disease, infiltrative disease and acute liver injury.
topics: Biopsy: indications, limitations and non-invasive alternatives
Social determinants, access and diagnostic uncertainty
boardDomains: Advanced Hepatology and Pretransplant (55%): cross-cutting diagnosis/testing; risk/prognosis; pathology and non-invasive assessment
units.casePractice: Use a linked AASLD pathology-pearls case to contrast a pattern description with an etiologic conclusion; explain what information would change the differential.
units.assessment: Short-answer pattern classification plus an annotated differential; rubric: pattern (2), discriminating tests (3), uncertainty/safety (2), evidence citation (3).

units.title: Cirrhosis, portal hypertension and decompensation
objectives: Organize evaluation of ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and renal dysfunction.
Compare portal-hypertension strategies and identify when multidisciplinary TIPS/transplant evaluation is indicated.
Explain how precipitating causes and organ dysfunction shape prognosis.
boardDomains: Advanced Hepatology and Pretransplant: portal hypertension complications (7%); palliative care (2%)
units.casePractice: Construct a decision tree for fictional decompensated cirrhosis with new ascites; state competing diagnoses and escalation thresholds, not a patient-specific order set.
units.assessment: Oral case map; rubric: syndrome recognition (25%), differential/trigger (25%), evidence-aligned management options (30%), safety and follow-up (20%).

units.title: Acute liver failure, ACLF and critical illness
objectives: Distinguish acute liver failure from acute-on-chronic liver failure using accepted clinical criteria and context.
Identify urgent transfer/consultation needs and structured etiologic work-up.
Reason about multiorgan dysfunction, prognosis, transplant assessment and palliative communication without making deterministic predictions.
boardDomains: Advanced Hepatology and Pretransplant: acute liver failure (4%); ACLF (<2%)
units.casePractice: Fictional time-sequenced case: map immediate stabilization, toxin/etiology tests, transplant-center discussion and uncertainty; no medication dosing or procedural instruction.
units.assessment: Timed prioritization exercise; rubric: urgency (30%), differential/tests (25%), referral/coordination (25%), communication/uncertainty (20%).

units.title: Viral, autoimmune and cholestatic liver disease
objectives: Interpret serologic and virologic results in context and identify reactivation/transplant implications.
Compare autoimmune hepatitis, PBC, PSC and overlap differentials without relying on one marker alone.
Plan pre- and post-transplant risk questions using current guidance and specialist input.
boardDomains: Advanced Hepatology and Pretransplant: viral hepatitis (3%); autoimmune disorders (7%); health maintenance (3%)
Post-transplant: recurrence and infection
units.casePractice: Compare fictional serology patterns and write what additional testing is needed before labeling disease or changing immunosuppression.
units.assessment: Case-based interpretation; rubric: appropriate interpretation (40%), differential (25%), transplant relevance (20%), guideline/date caveat (15%).

units.title: Metabolic, alcohol-associated, drug-induced and genetic disease
objectives: Compare common chronic liver disease etiologies and identify high-yield red flags for alternative diagnoses.
Review DILI causality as a structured diagnosis of exclusion and avoid unsupported attribution.
Integrate comorbidity, alcohol-use disorder, nutrition and transplant evaluation without stigma.
topics: Drug, herbal and supplement-induced liver injury
Wilson disease, hemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and other genetic disease
boardDomains: Advanced Hepatology and Pretransplant: genetic liver disease (4%); ALD (3%); MASLD/MASH/MetALD (4%); DILI (<2%)
units.casePractice: Use a fictional abnormal-liver-tests scenario to rank hypotheses and specify exposure timeline, labs and competing causes; avoid inferring causality from temporal association alone.
units.assessment: Structured differential memo; rubric: evidence use (30%), alternate causes (30%), non-stigmatizing contextual reasoning (20%), concise plan and safety (20%).

units.title: Vascular, congestive, pregnancy-related and pediatric disorders
objectives: Recognize vascular and cardiac causes of liver injury and portal hypertension.
Separate portal-vein thrombosis, Budd–Chiari, sinusoidal obstruction and congestive hepatopathy patterns.
Identify pregnancy-related or pediatric/congenital presentations needing specialty collaboration.
topics: Portal vein and splanchnic vascular disorders
Budd–Chiari, PSVD/NRH, SOS and Fontan-associated disease
Biliary atresia and pediatric transplant principles
boardDomains: Advanced Hepatology and Pretransplant: congestive hepatopathy (3%), vascular disease (2%), pregnancy (<2%), biliary atresia (<2%)
units.casePractice: Compare fictional Doppler/imaging descriptions and clinical contexts; link to official images/cases only where rights permit and do not download/rehost.
units.assessment: Concept map; rubric: anatomic reasoning (35%), differential (30%), relevant next tests (20%), referral boundaries (15%).

units.title: Liver tumors, HCC and transplant oncology
objectives: Distinguish surveillance, diagnostic imaging criteria and staging questions from treatment selection.
Discuss HCC and cholangiocarcinoma approaches in transplant and non-transplant settings.
Use tumor burden, liver reserve, performance status and multidisciplinary context without assuming a single modality is universally appropriate.
topics: Resection, locoregional/systemic approaches and transplant evaluation
boardDomains: Advanced Hepatology and Pretransplant: liver tumors (5%)
Post-transplant: recurrence of disease (3%)
units.casePractice: Review a linked AASLD pathology case and a publicly linked Radiopaedia case, if permitted; learners make a differential from supplied descriptors, not copied patient images.
units.assessment: Tumor-board brief; rubric: stage/eligibility concepts (25%), multidisciplinary differential (25%), options/risks (30%), source date and uncertainty (20%).

units.title: Transplant referral, candidate selection, donor evaluation and ethics
objectives: Describe evaluation domains for transplant candidates and deceased/living donors.
Recognize that allocation, exceptions, contraindications and center policies are time-sensitive and jurisdiction-specific.
Apply transparent, non-stigmatizing ethical reasoning to psychosocial risk, equity and organ stewardship.
topics: Deceased donor and living donor selection
Psychosocial assessment, substance-use disorder and equity
Ethics, informed consent and regulatory issues
boardDomains: Advanced Hepatology and Pretransplant: transplant selection/evaluation (3%)
Peritransplant (14%): donor selection, compatibility, ethics and organ policy (5% overall ethics/regulatory)
units.casePractice: Structured fictional candidate conference simulation with competing medical, psychosocial, donor, policy and equity factors; no fabricated listing decision.
units.assessment: One-page selection conference summary; rubric: completeness (25%), evidence/policy distinction (25%), ethics/equity (25%), transparent uncertainty (25%).

units.title: Peritransplant care and early complications
objectives: Organize immediate perioperative complication differentials by vascular, biliary, infectious and systemic mechanisms.
Interpret early allograft dysfunction as requiring a structured evaluation, not an assumed diagnosis.
Explain multidisciplinary roles and the need for supervised clinical judgment.
topics: Primary nonfunction and early allograft dysfunction
boardDomains: Peritransplant: perioperative complications (5%); donor transmission (2%); donor selection
units.casePractice: Use authentic public Radiopaedia liver-transplant case links only; image interpretation occurs on source platform, and redistribution requires license compliance.
units.assessment: Differential/next-step worksheet; rubric: vascular-biliary-infectious breadth (40%), clinical urgency (25%), appropriate referral/escalation (20%), source use (15%).

units.title: Allograft pathology, rejection and transplant immunology
objectives: Describe immune and non-immune causes of graft dysfunction and a staged diagnostic approach.
Relate histopathology, serology, drug exposure and time since transplant without diagnosing from one finding.
Explain core immunosuppressant mechanisms, adverse effects and interactions at a conceptual board-study level.
topics: Recurrent disease versus rejection versus infection
boardDomains: Transplant immunology (6%); post-transplant immune complications (4%); nonimmune complications (2%)
units.casePractice: Study AASLD Pathology Pearls cases on the publisher site; do not copy or redistribute their patient images or assume a teaching case substitutes for pathology supervision.
units.assessment: Mechanism map and fictional allograft dysfunction differential; rubric: competing causes (35%), test interpretation (30%), pharmacology/safety (20%), evidence limitations (15%).

units.title: Long-term transplant medicine, infection and recurrence
objectives: Structure post-transplant differential diagnosis across immune, infectious, biliary/vascular, medication and recurrent-disease causes.
Plan conceptual health-maintenance questions for malignancy, vaccination, metabolic and reproductive health.
Recognize interactions and when to consult transplant pharmacy/infectious-disease teams.
topics: Malignancy, metabolic health, vaccination and reproductive care
boardDomains: Post-transplant: infection (3%), recurrence (3%), health maintenance (3%); immunosuppression pharmacology (5%)
units.casePractice: Fictional late allograft dysfunction scenario requiring a ranked differential and a list of contextual medication/infection questions, not a prescription.
units.assessment: Case discussion; rubric: differential breadth (30%), interaction/infection reasoning (30%), prevention and equity (20%), escalation/citations (20%).

units.title: Professional practice, evidence appraisal and board-style synthesis
objectives: Interpret ABIM blueprint weights and select the task demanded by a clinical vignette.
Appraise guideline currency, evidence strength, applicability and conflicting recommendations.
Communicate uncertainty, patient goals and system limitations in a concise conference presentation.
boardDomains: All blueprint sections; diagnosis/testing 30%, treatment/care decisions 45%, prognosis/epidemiology 18%, basic science 7%
units.casePractice: Prepare an evidence-aware oral case conference from a fictional scenario; cite source dates and state what remains unknown.
units.assessment: Capstone board-style discussion; rubric: clinical reasoning (35%), source appraisal (25%), communication/team systems (20%), safety/equity/uncertainty (20%).

assignment.title: Longitudinal transplant-hepatology case-conference portfolio
assignment.instructions: Submit three fictional or appropriately linked public teaching cases: one pretransplant/chronic liver disease, one peritransplant, and one post-transplant. For each, map symptoms, data, differential, risk/prognosis, management options, consults, ethics/equity issues and the relevant ABIM blueprint code. Cite current public guidance and record access date. Do not use identifiable patient data, reproduce protected images, give patient-specific care recommendations, or claim competence from the exercise.
assignment.passThreshold: No validated pass threshold; formative self-study only. Feedback should identify missed reasoning steps, not predict board performance.

components: 12 unit formative checks and case maps
10 original practice questions with cited rationales
assessment.grading: Self-assessment/formative only. The questions are original educational material, not official ABIM/ABP items and not a validated predictor of certification or passing.

studyHours.basis: Illustrative 12-week study plan at 15 hours/week: 6 hours reading/notes, 4 hours case reasoning, 3 hours review/questions, 2 hours spaced retrieval weekly. Not clinical training hours and not evidence of readiness.

mapping.institution: Massachusetts General Hospital
mapping.name: MGH Advanced Hepatology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page calls this advanced training in liver disease and describes care of transplant candidates and recipients, a reported nine months on inpatient liver service, weekly hepatology and post-transplant clinics, endoscopy/biopsy exposure, regular conferences, and a longitudinal independent research project. It claims preparation for ABIM transplant-hepatology added-qualification requirements. Page carries a historical 2016 application deadline; its current accreditation/availability is not established here. Its claims about experience of 20+ post-transplant patients are programme-page descriptions, not a learner outcome or guarantee.

topicGaps: No public recording located in this pass had an authoritative, reproducible player duration that could be observed; the four relevant public video pages added to unknownDurationItems have transcript/page evidence only. No newly discovered recording is counted. Existing unknown items remain uncounted.

Public sources with free recordings do not provide adequately verified open runtime evidence in the stateless fetch environment. AASLD course catalog media remain sign-in gated and duration-opaque; no access workaround was attempted.

Verified open video coverage remains inadequate across all 12 mapped units, especially donor selection/policy/ethics, perioperative care, rejection/allograft dysfunction, immunosuppressant pharmacology and post-transplant infection/prevention.

The authored episodes and existing originalClipPlan are scripts/plans only: none has been recorded, clinically reviewed, rendered, uploaded or counted toward the 36-hour video target. The residual verified-recording gap is the full 36.0 hours; feasibility of filling it with genuinely relevant, duration-verifiable free recordings is not established.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.
