boardNames: ABIM Transplant Hepatology Certification Examination (jointly developed by ABIM and ABP; ABIM administers for ABIM candidates)
ABIM Gastroenterology certification (required before ABIM Transplant Hepatology examination application)
medical.boardStatus: Transplant hepatology is an ABIM/ABP subspecialty certification with a separate Transplant Hepatology Certification Examination. 'Advanced hepatology' is the MGH programme label, not itself a distinct board or separate board examination. The ABIM pathway requires prior ABIM Gastroenterology certification, qualifying formal accredited training, clinical competence and unrestricted licensure. ABP candidates must verify the separate ABP eligibility pathway directly with ABP.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The MGH public fellowship page describes a clinical advanced fellowship after a three-year gastroenterology fellowship and says its goal is qualification to sit for transplant-hepatology certification; it also reports an old August 1, 2016 application deadline. The page does not establish the programme's current ACGME accreditation, current openings, current appointment rules, or a particular learner's eligibility. ABIM's current published policy requires accredited/recognized transplant-hepatology training and prior ABIM Gastroenterology certification for the ABIM exam. Confirm current programme accreditation and track documentation directly with ACGME, MGH, ABIM or ABP before relying on exam eligibility. No guarantee is made.

officialProgrammes.institution: Massachusetts General Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: MGH Advanced Hepatology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page calls this advanced training in liver disease and describes care of transplant candidates and recipients, a reported nine months on inpatient liver service, weekly hepatology and post-transplant clinics, endoscopy/biopsy exposure, regular conferences, and a longitudinal independent research project. It claims preparation for ABIM transplant-hepatology added-qualification requirements. Page carries a historical 2016 application deadline; its current accreditation/availability is not established here. Its claims about experience of 20+ post-transplant patients are programme-page descriptions, not a learner outcome or guarantee.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One exact institutional variant is supplied by the item packet. The MGH source describes a real physician clinical fellowship (not merely a directory category or research-only postdoctoral supplement), with clinical service, clinic, procedural exposure and an independent research project as one component. The official designation is Advanced Hepatology Fellowship; transplant hepatology is the relevant ACGME/ABIM/ABP subspecialty framework. No other institutional variant was added because none is in the packet and this task is limited to MED-X021. MGH's current ACGME accreditation status and whether this named track is currently active could not be independently resolved from public sources; do not infer it from the page's historic eligibility language. No combined GI/TH institutional track is asserted for MGH. ACGME and AASLD recognize optional dual GI/TH pathways at programs that meet the pathway requirements, but a generic pathway is not evidence that this MGH variant offers one.
sourceCaveats: MGH's official page is a useful institutional description, but it displays an expired 2016 application deadline. It does not establish current operation or current ACGME accreditation of this named fellowship; independently verify with the institutions/boards.

The MGH page uses an older term, Certificate of Added Qualification, and lists historical requirements. Current ABIM describes a Transplant Hepatology Certification Examination with updated pathway requirements; current board policy prevails over legacy webpage wording.
ABIM policy reviewed on 2026-10-07 and ABIM blueprint dated January 2026 with detailed topic outline applicable beginning Fall 2026. Board policies and guidelines may change; re-check at use.

AASLD guidelines are copyright protected and may be inactive or superseded; its index advises caution for guidance not updated within five years. Check each item date and current guidance before relying on it.

External lecture runtimes were not verifiably obtained: stateless YouTube fetch returned transcript text but not authoritative player duration metadata; direct metadata extraction was bot-blocked. No authentication was attempted. Videos/course listings are excluded from counted hours until exact duration and free playback are observed.

This course is independent educational self-study, not Harvard/MGH/Johns Hopkins-affiliated, ACGME-accredited, supervised fellowship, licensure, board-eligibility determination, procedure credentialing, or a predictor/guarantee of exam success. Clinical review was not performed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner reviews the ABIM Transplant Hepatology Blueprint dated January 2026. Which task category carries the largest target proportion?

options.text: Diagnosis/testing
Treatment/care decisions
Risk assessment/prognosis/epidemiology
Pathophysiology/basic science

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint lists treatment/care decisions at 45%, versus diagnosis/testing 30%, risk/prognosis/epidemiology 18%, and basic science 7%. This is a blueprint allocation, not a predicted score or study guarantee.

practiceQuestions.stem: A physician asks whether an 'Advanced Hepatology Fellowship' title alone establishes ABIM transplant-hepatology exam eligibility. What is the best answer?

options.text: Yes; the local programme title establishes board eligibility.
Yes, if the fellow has viewed a board-review course.
No; eligibility depends on current ABIM requirements, qualifying training/accreditation, prior ABIM GI certification, competence and licensure.
No; transplant hepatology has no certification exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM policy specifies prior ABIM Gastroenterology certification, formal qualifying training, clinical competence and unrestricted licensure, and a separate exam. A programme title or self-study alone does not establish eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional adult with cirrhosis presents with new clinically apparent ascites. Which approach best reflects safe diagnostic reasoning?

options.text: Assume portal hypertension and defer evaluation unless fever develops.
Assess acuity and complications, consider competing causes, and use current guidance to determine diagnostic evaluation including fluid analysis when indicated.
Use a single serum marker to diagnose the cause.
Proceed directly to a transplant listing decision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: New ascites requires clinical assessment for infection, renal dysfunction, cardiopulmonary and other etiologies, and guideline-directed testing. No single marker or history item substitutes for evaluation; transplant candidacy is multidisciplinary and not determined by this vignette alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional transplant recipient develops graft dysfunction. Which is the most defensible initial conceptual framework?

options.text: Treat as rejection without further evaluation.
Consider immune and nonimmune causes, including vascular/biliary, infection, medication effects and recurrent disease, in context of timing and data.
Assume a high immunosuppressant level excludes infection.
Use biopsy appearance alone without clinical context.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Allograft dysfunction has a broad differential. Clinical timing, imaging, laboratory, microbiology, medication history and pathology are integrated; neither rejection nor another cause should be presumed from one clue.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has chronic hepatitis B and is being considered for transplant with future immunosuppression. Which principle should guide planning?

options.text: Ignore HBV status once transplantation is planned.
Assess viral status and reactivation/transmission risk using current HBV guidance and transplant-team planning.
Use antibody status alone to select immunosuppression.
Defer all HBV assessment until after transplantation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: HBV diagnosis, prophylaxis/monitoring considerations and transplant/immunosuppression context require current guidance and specialist planning; these choices are not settled by an isolated marker.

practiceQuestions.stem: A liver biopsy image is available in an AASLD Liver Fellow Network pathology teaching case. Which use is appropriate for this independent course?

options.text: Download and embed the image in a course handout because it is free to view.
Link learners to the source page, follow its terms, and do not reproduce the image absent permission or a clear applicable license.
Remove the patient label and assume all reuse rights.
Copy the entire case text into new practice questions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free viewing is not a license to rehost. AASLD content is copyright-protected unless a resource specifies otherwise; link to the original and respect case-specific rights and de-identification conditions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is preparing a teaching slide using a Radiopaedia liver-transplant case in a public, noncommercial tutorial. Which condition is central under Radiopaedia's stated license overview?

options.text: No attribution is needed if the content is educational.
Attribute the case, preserve the same license where sharing derivatives, and keep use noncommercial; review the full terms.
The case may be included in a paid course without asking.
All image rights transfer to the teacher.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia describes CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 for cases, requiring attribution, share-alike and noncommercial use, subject to its full Terms. A paid course/paywall is explicitly outside routine permission.
practiceQuestions.domain: Image rights and lawful educational use

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has abnormal liver tests after a new supplement. Which is the best general educational approach to suspected DILI?

options.text: Assume causality solely because the exposure came first.
Use a structured assessment of timing and phenotype while evaluating competing causes and severity.
Ignore nonprescription products.
Diagnose DILI from an isolated enzyme value.

practiceQuestions.rationale: DILI assessment includes medication/supplement history and timing, biochemical pattern, exclusion of alternative causes, severity and follow-up; temporal association alone does not prove causality.

practiceQuestions.stem: An institutional fellowship page says its historic goal was to prepare fellows for a transplant-hepatology certificate. The page has an expired 2016 deadline and no current accreditation statement. What should a learner conclude?

The page is useful evidence of the institution's stated historical programme, but current activity/accreditation must be verified independently.
The programme must be research-only.
The old deadline invalidates all clinical curriculum content.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official MGH page describes clinical curriculum but its deadline is historical and it does not establish current accreditation/current availability. Current ACGME/ABIM/MGH confirmation is necessary.

practiceQuestions.stem: A transplant-hepatology online catalog lists a $0 price, but its course player requires sign-in and no video runtimes are visible. What is the correct accounting?

Count only the stated credit-hours as recorded video duration.
Do not count hours until anonymously accessible recordings and exact runtimes are verified; document sign-in and unknown duration.
Estimate duration from the number of modules.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official catalog lists a $0 price, while the course page prompts sign-in and provides no observed lecture durations. Cost, access to the catalog, and verified public video runtime are different evidence fields; unknown duration contributes no counted video time.

title: Neurorecovery Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional Neurorecovery track; not classified as an ACGME Brain Injury Medicine fellowship on the public page)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Completed residency-level education in Neurology or Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation; the institutional eligibility statement, board rules, and licensing requirements must be checked for current recruitment cycle.
Working knowledge of adult neurology, stroke, traumatic and spinal cord injury, basic rehabilitation medicine, clinical outcome measures, and evidence appraisal.
This course is advanced self-study; it is not prerequisite credit for a fellowship or board examination.
objectives: Explain the continuum from acute neurological injury through inpatient, outpatient, and community recovery, with realistic uncertainty.
Organize common neurorecovery problems by etiology, impairment, activity, participation, and systemic/psychosocial sequelae.
Map relevant knowledge to the published 2026 ABPMR BIM content outline while distinguishing it from the MGB Neurorecovery programme curriculum.
Critically evaluate clinical guidelines, single-patient reports, outcomes, and emerging technologies.
Communicate learning cases with source-based reasoning, shared goals, scope limits, and explicit unknowns.

units.title: Neurorecovery framework, injury mechanisms, and functional prognosis
objectives: Distinguish neurorecovery/neurorehabilitation from acute disease treatment and from the named MGB clinical-research fellowship.
Relate injury mechanism and lesion burden to impairment, activity, participation, and environmental context without deterministic prognosis.
Use serial, validated measures and communicate uncertainty in recovery trajectories.
topics: Neuroplasticity, restitution, compensation, spontaneous recovery, and learning-dependent change
Stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, anoxia/hypoxia, status epilepticus, and other acute neurologic injuries
ICF framework; baseline, impairment, activity, participation, and patient-prioritized goals
Measurement properties, meaningful change, confounding, and selection bias

Recovery is not a single biological curve: distinguish spontaneous change, task-specific learning, restitution of a function, and compensation in activity; these labels describe different explanatory levels, not competing diagnoses.
Interpret repeated outcomes in light of baseline ability, opportunity to practice, fatigue, context, and measurement error; a change score is not itself an individual prognosis.
Separate a research measure from a personally meaningful activity or participation outcome; record whose goal defines success.
boardDomains: Etiologies: vascular; moderate/severe TBI; anoxic/hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
A. Central nervous system manifestations (30%); B. Cognitive/behavioral dysfunction (20%)
units.casePractice: Fictional case: construct a problem representation and a three-domain outcomes plan for an adult recovering after a hemispheric stroke; explicitly list prognostic uncertainty.
units.assessment: One-page ICF-based formulation; rubric: accurate mechanism (25%), impairment/activity/participation distinction (25%), valid measure selection (25%), calibrated uncertainty and goals (25%).

units.title: Acute-to-postacute transitions, consultation, and care systems
objectives: Compare acute inpatient, inpatient rehabilitation, skilled nursing, outpatient, and home rehabilitation at a conceptual level.
Prioritize medical stability, participation capacity, safety, support, and service needs rather than choosing a setting from diagnosis alone.
Produce a safe handoff that conveys function, precautions, pending issues, goals, and follow-up.
topics: Continuum of care and rehabilitation consultations
Interprofessional roles and shared goal setting
Discharge transitions, access inequities, caregiver capacity, and health literacy

A transition note should state current medical and functional status, communication needs, precautions supplied by the treating team, goals, pending evaluations, responsible follow-up, and escalation contacts; the note cannot itself establish placement eligibility.

Compare settings by service intensity and capacity to meet needs, not by diagnosis label; local payer criteria, bed availability, geography, disability access, and caregiver resources constrain real options.
Treat handoff as a safety intervention: use teach-back and confirm responsibility for unresolved issues rather than assuming that sending a document completes continuity.
boardDomains: F. Systemic manifestations (15%); A. CNS manifestations (30%)
Tasks across etiologies: prevention, evaluation/diagnosis, prognosis, rehabilitative management, education
units.casePractice: Fictional transition vignette: create a handoff checklist for a medically stable person with residual aphasia and mobility limitations; identify information still needed before placement recommendation.
units.assessment: Structured handoff; rubric: critical medical issues (30%), functional description (25%), interdisciplinary communication (25%), explicit unknowns/contingencies (20%).

units.title: Stroke recovery: assessment, activity-based therapy, and secondary consequences
objectives: Map stroke-related impairments to activity-limited goals and identify sources of evidence for the current rehabilitation plan.
Describe restorative and compensatory approaches and why multidisciplinary coordination matters.
Screen for common communication, swallowing, mood, pain, sleep, and mobility consequences.
topics: Ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke recovery in the rehabilitation continuum
Motor, upper-limb, gait/balance, aphasia, dysarthria, dysphagia, vision, and cognition
Dose, timing, task-specific practice, telerehabilitation, and evidence limitations
2026 AHA/ASA adult stroke rehabilitation guideline and update dates
For each stroke-related goal, link impairment, task practice, and participation; distinguish impairment improvement from transfer to daily activities and from compensation.
Interpret treatment timing and dose in the context of the 2026 adult guideline: rehabilitation should begin in the acute phase, while best approach, timing, and dose remain uncertain in some domains.
Include communication, swallowing, mood, sensory, cognitive, sleep, and pain concerns in coordinated assessment; avoid reducing recovery to motor scores.
boardDomains: Etiology: vascular
A. CNS manifestations (30%); B. Cognitive/behavioral dysfunction (20%); C. Psychiatric manifestations (15%); D. Pain/sleep disorders (15%)
units.casePractice: Authentic published report for methodological critique only: the linked open case report describes post-stroke upper-limb BCI rehabilitation; distinguish case-level observation from efficacy evidence. Do not reproduce its images or patient-level details.
units.assessment: Guideline-to-case evidence map; rubric: source currency (25%), relevant domain coverage (25%), differentiation of established care from emerging technology (25%), limitations (25%).

units.title: Traumatic brain injury across severity and recovery phases
objectives: Organize TBI evaluation by severity/context and time course while recognizing that severity labels do not determine an individual outcome.
Identify common neurologic, cognitive-behavioral, psychiatric, pain/sleep, and systemic sequelae.
Critically apply post-acute mTBI guidance and distinguish its scope from moderate/severe TBI rehabilitation.
topics: Mild versus moderate/severe TBI and sports/non-sports contexts
Post-traumatic amnesia and serial cognition/behavior observations
Persistent symptoms, headache, dizziness, sleep, fatigue, mood, and participation
VA/DoD 2021 guideline scope: post-acute mTBI; check for newer local guidance

For persistent post-concussion symptoms, construct a symptom-domain differential including sleep, pain/headache, vestibular/visual, cognition, mood, medication, and environmental contributions; symptom checklists do not establish etiology.
Apply the VA/DoD 2021 guideline only to its stated post-acute mild-TBI population and local context; do not extrapolate its algorithms to moderate/severe TBI, acute trauma, or stroke.
For any worsening or concerning features, prioritize clinical reassessment and established escalation pathways over a rehabilitation self-study algorithm.
boardDomains: Etiologies A. Sports (mild TBI), B. Non-sports (mild TBI), C. Moderate/severe TBI, D. Blast injury
A–F sequelae categories in ABPMR BIM outline
units.casePractice: Fictional vignette: use a symptom-domain table to organize persistent post-concussion concerns, red flags, alternatives, and referral/reevaluation questions; do not diagnose from symptom scores alone.
units.assessment: Two-column evidence appraisal; rubric: guideline population match (30%), differential domains (30%), safety/escalation (20%), patient-centered communication (20%).

units.title: Spinal cord injury, neurologic level, function, and secondary prevention
objectives: Describe the relationship between neurologic impairment and function after SCI without equating level with individual capacity.
Identify high-priority autonomic, respiratory, bowel/bladder, skin, thromboembolic, pain, and participation issues for supervised clinical learning.
Use contemporary SCI guidance and recognize jurisdiction-specific protocols.
topics: Neurologic classification and functional assessment concepts
Respiratory, autonomic, bowel/bladder, skin, bone, pain, sexual health, and upper-limb preservation
CAN-SCIP living guideline and SCIRE/PVA resource access conditions
Use neurologic classification as a shared descriptive language, not a substitute for functional assessment or an inference that the same neurologic level yields identical capacity.
Organize SCI concerns by autonomic, respiratory, bowel/bladder, skin, bone, pain, sexual health, equipment, and participation domains; use current jurisdictional and team protocols.
Distinguish public guideline access from permission to reproduce resources; check topic-specific update dates and individual access terms in CAN-SCIP/SCIRE-linked material.
boardDomains: Etiology: traumatic brain injury overlap only where the BIM outline lists; cross-track neurorecovery topic, not a claim of BIM exam coverage for all SCI care
F. Systemic manifestations (15%); D. Pain/sleep (15%); E. Soft tissue/orthopedic (5%)
units.casePractice: Fictional SCI education vignette: prioritize which clinical domains require immediate team review; do not prescribe individualized emergency actions or perform procedures.
units.assessment: Risk/needs matrix; rubric: domain coverage (35%), safe prioritization (30%), source use (20%), uncertainty and scope statement (15%).

units.title: Disorders of consciousness and cognitive-motor dissociation
objectives: Differentiate coma, unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, and minimally conscious states at a conceptual bedside-assessment level.
Explain why serial standardized examination, confounder review, and team observation matter.
Summarize cognitive-motor dissociation as an active research topic without presenting experimental detection/intervention as standard care.
topics: Arousal versus awareness; behavioral diagnosis and confounds
Medication, medical instability, sensory/motor impairment, and communication limitations
Emerging neurotechnology, evidence limits, and research ethics
Arousal, awareness, and observable motor output are not interchangeable; sensory, language, motor, medication, medical, and environmental barriers can mask responses.
Use serial standardized examination and identify/treat confounders before high-stakes diagnostic or prognostic claims; one observation is a sample, not a trajectory.
Communicate prognosis in calibrated terms, separating group-level associations from an individual forecast and acknowledging the limits of behavioral and ancillary tests.
boardDomains: C. Moderate/severe TBI and F. anoxic/hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
A. CNS manifestations—disorders of consciousness; B. attention/arousal (20%)
units.casePractice: Fictional case: compare a serial observation record with a single examination; state the minimum additional information needed and avoid premature certainty.
units.assessment: Short-answer differential; rubric: state distinctions (35%), identify confounds (30%), serial assessment rationale (20%), calibrated language (15%).

units.title: Cognition, communication, behavior, and psychiatric sequelae
objectives: Organize acquired cognitive and behavioral complaints into testable domains and functional consequences.
Distinguish possible psychiatric, neurologic, medication, sleep, pain, and environmental contributions.
Plan an interdisciplinary assessment and communicate respectfully with patients and families.
topics: Attention, memory, executive function, agnosia, apathy, agitation, delirium, impulse control
Aphasia, articulation, swallowing, hearing, visual/vestibular symptoms
Adjustment, anxiety, depression, PTSD, psychosis, substance use, and functional symptoms
Neuropsychological assessment, decision making, capacity questions, health equity

Translate complaints into domains and functional consequences; assess plausible neurologic, psychiatric, medication, sleep, pain, sensory, communication, and contextual contributors in collaboration with appropriate disciplines.

Do not equate agitation, apathy, reduced participation, or inconsistent performance with intent or a single mechanism; use respectful, accessible communication and collateral information appropriately.
Capacity is decision-specific and time-sensitive; a course case can teach the question structure but cannot determine capacity for a real person.
boardDomains: B. Cognitive and behavioral dysfunction (20%); C. Psychiatric manifestations (15%); A. CNS manifestations (30%)
units.casePractice: Fictional interdisciplinary case conference: formulate symptom clusters and propose who should assess each domain; avoid attributing unexplained symptoms to a single mechanism.
units.assessment: Team formulation; rubric: breadth of differential (30%), role clarity (25%), functional relevance (25%), respectful uncertainty (20%).

units.title: Pain, sleep, fatigue, and sensory symptoms
objectives: Classify pain and sleep complaints by symptom pattern and possible neurologic/systemic contributors.
Recognize the overlap among fatigue, sleep-disordered breathing, mood, medication effects, and neurologic injury.
Identify when reassessment or specialist input is needed rather than escalating a single symptom label.
topics: Central and peripheral neuropathic pain, myofascial pain, headache/facial pain
Insomnia, hypersomnia, sleep breathing disorders, fatigue

Build a symptom interaction map before attributing fatigue or pain to injury: consider sleep disorders, mood, medication, deconditioning, sensory changes, pain, and systemic illness, then identify what information could distinguish them.

unitMap.text: Neurorecovery framework, injury mechanisms, and functional prognosis
coveredTopics: Neuroplasticity, restitution, compensation, spontaneous recovery, and learning-dependent change
Stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, anoxia/hypoxia, status epilepticus, and other acute neurologic injuries
ICF framework; baseline, impairment, activity, participation, and patient-prioritized goals
Measurement properties, meaningful change, confounding, and selection bias

Recovery is not a single biological curve: distinguish spontaneous change, task-specific learning, restitution of a function, and compensation in activity; these labels describe different explanatory levels, not competing diagnoses.
Interpret repeated outcomes in light of baseline ability, opportunity to practice, fatigue, context, and measurement error; a change score is not itself an individual prognosis.
Separate a research measure from a personally meaningful activity or participation outcome; record whose goal defines success.

unitMap.text: Acute-to-postacute transitions, consultation, and care systems
coveredTopics: Continuum of care and rehabilitation consultations

A transition note should state current medical and functional status, communication needs, precautions supplied by the treating team, goals, pending evaluations, responsible follow-up, and escalation contacts; the note cannot itself establish placement eligibility.

Compare settings by service intensity and capacity to meet needs, not by diagnosis label; local payer criteria, bed availability, geography, disability access, and caregiver resources constrain real options.
Treat handoff as a safety intervention: use teach-back and confirm responsibility for unresolved issues rather than assuming that sending a document completes continuity.

unitMap.text: Stroke recovery: assessment, activity-based therapy, and secondary consequences

2026 AHA/ASA adult stroke rehabilitation guideline and update dates
For each stroke-related goal, link impairment, task practice, and participation; distinguish impairment improvement from transfer to daily activities and from compensation.
Interpret treatment timing and dose in the context of the 2026 adult guideline: rehabilitation should begin in the acute phase, while best approach, timing, and dose remain uncertain in some domains.
Include communication, swallowing, mood, sensory, cognitive, sleep, and pain concerns in coordinated assessment; avoid reducing recovery to motor scores.

For persistent post-concussion symptoms, construct a symptom-domain differential including sleep, pain/headache, vestibular/visual, cognition, mood, medication, and environmental contributions; symptom checklists do not establish etiology.
Apply the VA/DoD 2021 guideline only to its stated post-acute mild-TBI population and local context; do not extrapolate its algorithms to moderate/severe TBI, acute trauma, or stroke.
For any worsening or concerning features, prioritize clinical reassessment and established escalation pathways over a rehabilitation self-study algorithm.

For a synthesis, state what is known, what is inferred, what is missing, and which additional information could change the formulation; do not fill gaps with assumed examination findings.
Map study prompts to the exact 2026 ABPMR BIM domains without conflating blueprint coverage with clinical fellowship curriculum or board eligibility.
A final learning plan should prioritize current sources and unresolved domains; no quiz, study-hour estimate, or independent course predicts examination success or clinical competence.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The MGB programme page says applicants should have completed Neurology or Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation residency and be board-eligible in one by June 30, 2026; its displayed Massachusetts full-license date is July 1, 2027. Completing this independent self-study course does not confer eligibility.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Official Mass General Brigham listings call MED-X022 a clinical physician fellowship in Neurology, with one-year clinical training and research opportunity. It is distinct from the separately listed Spaulding Rehabilitation Brain Injury Medicine fellowship, which the official page explicitly labels ACGME-accredited. No ACGME accreditation for the MED-X022 track itself was found on its official Neurorecovery page. A directory label is not an accreditation claim.
sourceCaveats: Human clinical review was not performed. Clinical sources and recommendations should be reviewed by qualified clinicians before use.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient recovering from a hemispheric stroke has reduced arm use. Which approach best supports a defensible functional treatment discussion?

options.text: Select an intervention from the impairment label alone.
Clarify the patient-prioritized activity goal, examine relevant contributors, and select a measure that can track that goal.
Assume all persistent weakness reflects fixed tissue damage.
Use an experimental technology before considering established rehabilitation options.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 stroke guideline frames rehabilitation as a combination of restorative and compensatory interventions and stresses coordinated, person-centered care; functional goal and measurement should drive reasoning, not label alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with post-acute mild TBI reports persistent fatigue, poor sleep, headache, and concentration difficulty. What is the most defensible first educational reasoning step?

options.text: Attribute every symptom to the injury without reassessment.
Organize complaints by symptom domain, evaluate potentially interacting contributors and red flags, and use current post-acute guidance matched to the population.
Use a single symptom score as a complete diagnosis.
Assume the 2021 VA/DoD guideline applies unchanged to all severities and settings.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The VA/DoD source is explicitly for post-acute mTBI and organizes recommendations by initial presentation and persisting symptoms. Symptom overlap warrants structured reassessment and population-matched guidance; do not generalize it to every TBI context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reads a single published case report of upper-limb gains during an experimental BCI rehabilitation intervention. Which inference is justified?

options.text: The device is proven effective for all people after stroke.
The observation is hypothesis-generating; a single case cannot establish comparative efficacy or generalizability.
The measured change proves the proposed neural mechanism.
Routine access and standard-of-care status are established.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A single case may illustrate feasibility and longitudinal measurements, but lacks a comparative counterfactual and cannot establish general effectiveness, mechanism, or routine-care status.
practiceQuestions.domain: Vascular etiology; rehabilitative management; emerging technology

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient recovering from stroke has new anxiety and low mood affecting therapy participation. Which course-level response is most consistent with current adult stroke rehabilitation guidance?

options.text: Ignore mood because rehabilitation concerns only motor function.
Include screening and appropriate assessment/management within coordinated multidisciplinary rehabilitation.
Assume the symptoms are evidence of poor motivation.
Use a neurologic impairment scale as a substitute for mental-health assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 AHA/ASA summary highlights screening and treatment for post-stroke depression and anxiety, as part of coordinated, multidisciplinary recovery. This is not a patient-specific treatment recommendation.

practiceQuestions.stem: During education about the ABPMR Brain Injury Medicine examination, which statement accurately describes the 2026 outline?

options.text: It is only a test of acute TBI diagnosis.
The outline includes etiologies and six sequelae domains; central nervous system manifestations carry 30% of the listed content distribution.
All patient ages are included without age qualification.
The outline is a guarantee that completing this course makes a learner eligible.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official 2026 effective outline lists six sequelae categories, with CNS manifestations at 30%; it notes patients age 15 and older. Exam eligibility depends on board requirements and approved training, not this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which interpretation correctly distinguishes the MGB Neurorecovery Fellowship from the Spaulding Brain Injury Medicine Fellowship?

options.text: They are interchangeable names for one ACGME-approved BIM training track.

The Neurorecovery programme describes a one-year clinical neurorecovery/neurorehabilitation fellowship with research and consult/ambulatory experience; the separate Spaulding BIM programme is expressly labeled ACGME-accredited.
The Neurorecovery programme is research-only.
The BIM programme is only a general neurology residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The MGB page describes clinical neurorecovery training and protected research time but does not label it ACGME-accredited. The separate Spaulding fellowship page expressly describes an ACGME-accredited BIM fellowship. Do not transfer accreditation or board-eligibility implications between programmes.

practiceQuestions.stem: A review is being planned for adult stroke rehabilitation recommendations. Which source is the most current among the linked course references as checked October 7, 2026?

options.text: The 2016 AHA/ASA stroke rehabilitation guideline as the only current source.
The 2026 AHA/ASA Guideline for Adult Stroke Rehabilitation and Recovery, updated August 27, 2026.
A 2021 guideline for post-acute mild TBI.
A web video with no visible publication date.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AHA professional page states that the 2026 guideline was updated August 27, 2026. Older or condition-specific guidelines can remain relevant within scope but do not supersede this newer stroke rehab guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teaching team is assessing a change after an experimental rehabilitation intervention. Which design feature best strengthens interpretation of the change?

options.text: Record only a post-intervention impairment score.
Predefine functional and impairment outcomes, time points, important confounders, and adverse-event monitoring, then interpret limitations.
Select whichever outcome changed most after treatment.
Infer mechanism from improvement alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Transparent prespecified outcome measurement and confounder tracking support interpretable research; neither pre/post change alone nor a single case can establish causality. NINDS describes common data elements and standardized outcomes as important to TBI research.

practiceQuestions.stem: The Neurorecovery Fellowship page states that its applicants should have completed residency in which fields and be board-eligible by June 30, 2026?

options.text: Neurology or physical medicine and rehabilitation
Neurosurgery only
Psychiatry or emergency medicine only
Any graduate degree

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official MGB programme page specifies completed Neurology or Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation residency and board eligibility in either by June 30, 2026. As checked October 7, 2026, this displayed date is past and likely cycle-specific; verify current recruitment requirements with the programme.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner asks whether completing an independent Neurorecovery course makes them eligible for Brain Injury Medicine certification. Which response is correct?

options.text: Yes, any neurorehabilitation course satisfies the board requirement.

No. Eligibility is determined by the certifying board; current board routes require underlying board certification and specified approved BIM fellowship training, and this self-study course confers neither.
Yes, if the learner passes the course quiz.
Eligibility is conferred by the university affiliation named in the course.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPMR/ABPN describe the separate BIM certification examination and specified training/board requirements. The MGB Neurorecovery programme is not expressly designated as ACGME BIM fellowship training on its public page, and independent self-study cannot confer eligibility.

topicGaps: The deduplicated ledger is 33 recordings (7.786389 hours): primarily EEG, plus one 37:21 introductory NCS/EMG video and one 46:41 spine-focused IONM lecture. These are useful topic additions, not a comprehensive physician-level sequence in either domain.

No free, public, duration-verified full lecture sequence was established for evoked potentials, polysomnography/sleep, autonomic testing, neuromuscular ultrasound, single-fiber EMG or movement-disorder neurophysiology. Search findings are not counted when gated, login-dependent, unavailable, insufficiently relevant, or without direct observed runtime.

Routine adult EEG reporting, comprehensive epilepsy monitoring, advanced EDX localization, and critical-care EEG still lack enough accessible lecture hours to support the 36-hour floor. The added hours do not close the large residual gap.
No public MGB didactic lecture recordings or course runtime are published in the checked official programme summaries; a 12-month ACGME fellowship requirement is not a video-hour count.
Some ACNS EP/IONM guidance is dated and must be checked against current society and local practice standards.
Linked authentic case resources may have unreviewed de-identification and reuse conditions; no patient image, trace, screenshot or case content was copied.

medical.boardStatus: YES — a separate ABPN Clinical Neurophysiology subspecialty certification examination exists. ABPN states that applicants must be certified in general neurology or neurology with special qualification in child neurology by the prior year, complete one year of ACGME-accredited CNP fellowship training after neurology residency, and meet the stated licensing/training requirements. The ABPN continuing-certification exam offers standard, EEG-emphasis, or EMG-emphasis options; these are not verified entry fellowship tracks or initial-exam outlines. The ABCN has a separate certification system. ABPN epilepsy certification is another separate subspecialty. Current requirements must be checked at ABPN; this independent course confers none of the eligibility conditions.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: No board eligibility is conferred. ABPN initial CNP certification requires board certification in general Neurology or Neurology with Special Qualification in Child Neurology, plus the required one-year ACGME-accredited CNP fellowship after residency, licensure and other current ABPN rules. MGB’s own entry requirements are a separate program admission matter. Verify with ABPN and program leadership; this independent course is not ACGME accredited, does not satisfy fellowship time, does not guarantee exam passing and is not official ABPN content.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet supplied one MGB physician CNP fellowship. Current official pages identify an integrated MGB training programme involving MGH and BWH with VA Boston as an affiliated experience; they do not establish separate MGH and BWH fellowships or distinct institution-specific tracks. The official page describes it as physician clinical fellowship rather than a generic directory category, but the full local schedule, ACGME ADS entry, exact rotations, duration by site and actual lecture hours were not independently confirmed. The 2025 ACGME standard says accredited CNP education is 12 months; the page’s two-year CNP→Epilepsy route is sequential training in two named subspecialties, not one two-year CNP fellowship or guarantee of two certifications. Research is encouraged as an optional scholarly supplement and is not substituted for clinical specialty training. No research-only/non-physician offering was added as a track.
sourceCaveats: The MGB pages are current institutional programme summaries, not a full public curriculum. MGB programme admission rules and ABPN certification rules differ; both are stated separately.

ACGME requirements define accredited programme standards, not proof that every listed topic is delivered at a named site or that this independent course is accredited. ACGME ADS listing was not independently verified.

The initial ABPN CNP page confirms the separate exam and eligibility requirements, but a topic-by-topic initial exam blueprint was not found in the checked public sources. The available ABPN CC blueprint is not treated as initial-exam blueprint.
Current programme pages say MGB has an integrated site structure; standalone BWH and MGH CNP pathways were not substantiated. The optional epilepsy second year is distinct from CNP.

Search findings are not counted when gated, login-dependent, unavailable, insufficiently relevant, or without direct observed runtime.

Routine adult EEG reporting, comprehensive epilepsy monitoring, advanced EDX localization, and critical-care EEG still lack enough accessible lecture hours to support the 36-hour floor. The added hours do not close the large residual gap.

practiceQuestions.stem: A routine EEG shows a clear posterior rhythm during relaxed wakefulness that attenuates with eye opening. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: A normal physiologic reactivity feature should be described in the context of age and state.
This alone establishes a focal seizure disorder.
It is proof of a structural occipital lesion.
It establishes a normal neurologic examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Eye opening can attenuate the posterior dominant rhythm; this is a physiologic feature, not a stand-alone disease diagnosis or proof of normal examination. Age, state and recording quality matter.
practiceQuestions.domain: EEG normal physiology and report reasoning

practiceQuestions.stem: During review, sharp transients appear time-locked to movement and occur with abrupt baseline shifts in several channels. What is the best next step?

options.text: Call the pattern generalized epileptiform activity immediately.
Review video, channel field, montage and technical context before classifying the waveform.
Ignore all transients whenever movement occurs.
Diagnose an electrographic seizure based on shape alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Artifact identification requires context, field, timing and technical review. A stereotyped sharp shape alone does not establish an epileptiform discharge.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 10-year-old’s EEG contains a pattern that would be unusual in an awake adult. What principle should guide the interpretation?

options.text: Use adult criteria unchanged to avoid age bias.
Consider age, state and development and compare against an age-appropriate reference.
Assume every age-specific pattern is abnormal.
Diagnose epilepsy from any sharply contoured waveform.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Normal EEG changes with development and state; age-appropriate interpretation is essential. The question does not name a pattern so no diagnosis can be made.

practiceQuestions.stem: A brief routine EEG contains no seizure, but intermittent stereotyped spells continue clinically. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: Epilepsy is excluded.
The brief recording did not capture an electrographic seizure; its sampling limits should be stated and the clinical team may consider further monitoring.
A seizure diagnosis is confirmed despite no EEG change.
The EEG should be repeated indefinitely until a seizure appears.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A short routine study is a sample and cannot exclude every intermittent event. Test choice and follow-up depend on the clinical question and responsible team; no single strategy is mandatory from this vignette alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: In ACNS critical-care EEG terminology, why should a rhythmic/periodic pattern description be kept distinct from a clinical treatment decision?

options.text: Terminology standardizes description; clinical significance and management require the broader context and responsible team.
Every periodic pattern is a seizure.
A terminology label proves tissue injury.
No EEG terminology can be used in ICU patients.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACNS terminology provides standardized nomenclature and associated descriptors. It is not, by itself, a treatment protocol or diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A focal sensory complaint leads to consideration of radiculopathy versus a distal mononeuropathy. What is the best planning approach before NCS/needle EMG?

options.text: Perform an identical full study on every referral.
State the clinical localization/differential and design a focused electrodiagnostic plan, acknowledging sampling and timing limits.
Choose the most uncomfortable test first.
Use one normal sensory response to exclude every root lesion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME explicitly calls for competence in developing and executing an appropriate electrodiagnostic plan. Test choice is hypothesis-driven and findings require context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about routine nerve conduction measurements is most appropriate?

options.text: An isolated latency value determines the lesion location irrespective of temperature or distance.
Interpret latency, amplitude and velocity with distances, temperature, technique, reference ranges and clinical context.
A normal NCS excludes all small-fiber disorders and radiculopathies.
Needle EMG is unnecessary whenever NCS is performed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: EDX measures are technical and sampling-dependent; no single normal response rules out every peripheral nervous system disorder.

practiceQuestions.stem: During IONM, an SSEP amplitude change is reported. Which response is most appropriate educationally?

options.text: Declare a surgical cord injury from that signal alone.
Systematically check technical and physiologic factors, compare other modalities, promptly communicate the change and let the clinical team interpret in context.
Ignore it if the patient is under anesthesia.
Apply one universal threshold regardless of modality or protocol.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IONM changes require quality checks, context, multimodal integration and timely communication. The cited case itself shows why a signal alone does not establish a specific lesion; thresholds are protocol-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which item is expressly part of the ACGME CNP didactic curriculum even when a local program emphasizes another modality?

options.text: Neuromuscular ultrasound.
A guaranteed independent practice license.
A specific number of procedures in this independent online course.
A guaranteed ABPN exam pass.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current ACGME program requirements list neuromuscular ultrasound among broad educational components. ACGME program expectations are not authority to award licensure, procedural privileges, or a board pass.
practiceQuestions.domain: ACGME program curriculum vs independent course scope

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes an MGB CNP fellowship from the independent course described here?

options.text: Completing this online course establishes eligibility for the ABPN CNP examination.
ABPN CNP certification requires its own primary-board and ACGME training conditions; this course is unaffiliated and provides neither accredited fellowship training nor board eligibility.
The ABPN CNP examination is the same as the neurology primary board examination.
A planned original video counts as a fellowship rotation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPN lists a distinct CNP subspecialty certification and requires neurology/child neurology board status plus one year of ACGME-accredited CNP fellowship training. Independent educational materials confer none of those conditions.

title: Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (adult); official MGB page identifies distinct clinical and clinical-research tracks; educational course is not a fellowship-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Neurology residency-level clinical foundations; MGB states applicants should have completed accredited neurology residency.
Working knowledge of neuroanatomy, neurologic examination, MRI/CSF interpretation and evidence-based practice.
This is advanced self-study, not entry-to-practice training; no patient care, procedures or clinical access.
objectives: Synthesize clinical phenotype, MRI, CSF and biomarkers using current MS/NID criteria and explicit differential diagnoses.
Distinguish MS from AQP4-IgG-positive/negative NMOSD, MOGAD and selected mimics without overinterpreting isolated tests.
Explain DMT mechanisms, individualized choice and safety-monitoring concepts using dated authoritative sources.
Design a multidisciplinary, person-centered learning plan covering symptoms, function, life course, equity and evidence appraisal.

topicGaps: Progression independent of relapse activity, progressive MS and advanced disease: existing foundation lecture, but limited dedicated modern teaching and insufficient recorded depth.

MOGAD: differential coverage exists in NMOSD grand rounds, but proposed criteria/validation and low-pretest-probability interpretation lack a dedicated full lecture.
Acute MS relapse assessment, pseudo-relapse and rescue: NMOSD rescue lecture is relevant but not an MS relapse protocol; current MS acute-care source review needed.
Current MS DMT mechanisms, comparative safety, switching/discontinuation, vaccination/infection, pregnancy: no complete 2024-2026 MS DMT lecture verified; NMOSD therapeutics are not a substitute.
Rare autoimmune encephalitis, CNS vasculitis and systemic inflammatory mimics: only curriculum and reading coverage; no verified full lectures found.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One adult physician subspecialty fellowship with distinct clinical and clinical-research tracks. Not a generic taxonomy entry, not a combined adult/pediatric programme, not research-only postdoctoral employment and not a non-physician curriculum. The pediatric MGB MS/demyelinating fellowship is a separate institutional offering (MED-X018) and is intentionally excluded. MGB marks this opportunity Non-GME; do not assert ACGME accreditation. Clinical research track remains a physician fellowship with clinical activity, not the same as a research-only postdoc. MGB’s clinical rotation/case percentages are the programme’s own published description; they are not independently audited or guarantees.
sourceCaveats: MGB programme page is marked Non-GME and its posted curriculum is institution-authored, not an independent accreditation audit.
No distinct ABMS/ABPN/UCNS MS-Neuroimmunology board exam was listed on the official UCNS pages checked; confirm with relevant boards if the credential landscape changes.
The 2024 McDonald criteria are a 2024 revision published in 2025; older lectures may predate them.
AAN DMT guideline is from 2018 and explicitly describes a rapidly changing treatment field; use it for framework, not current drug-label details.
MOGAD diagnostic criteria are proposed consensus criteria and the literature notes validation needs; interpret using phenotype and assay.

YouTube public playlist offers five counted specialty lecture recordings totaling observed 11,007 seconds; Stanford 10:09 explainer excluded. Runtime/public page evidence does not establish current downloadable rights or guarantee continued availability.
Case images and records are not copied. Source access is not reuse permission; protected images must not be rehosted.

The independent curriculum does not provide accredited supervised clinical training, patient care, case logs, procedures, licensure, board eligibility or certification. Human clinical review has not been performed.
Any future clinical guidance must be checked against current local standards, regulators, product labels, patient-specific contraindications and specialist judgment.

No separate MS/NI board certification is identified in the course packet; mapped competencies remain parent neurology knowledge and consensus fellowship competencies, not a board blueprint.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 29-year-old has painful unilateral subacute visual loss, dyschromatopsia and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Which next reasoning step is most appropriate?

options.text: Assume MS from the optic neuritis syndrome alone.
Localize an optic neuropathy, assess atypical features and integrate orbital/brain imaging with the differential.
Order MOG-IgG in every patient with any visual symptom.
Start a DMT before obtaining a neurologic history.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The syndrome is compatible with optic neuritis but not by itself proof of MS. Integrate clinical pattern, imaging and alternative causes; test selection should be phenotype-driven.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately reflects the 2024 McDonald revisions published in 2025?

options.text: Optic nerve is now a fifth anatomical location; CVS, PRL and CSF kFLC can provide supportive evidence in defined contexts.
Any positive MOG-IgG establishes MS.
MRI lesions alone always establish MS.
A single nonspecific symptom is sufficient if MRI has white matter spots.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The revised criteria added the optic nerve as a fifth location and allow selected biomarkers as supportive evidence; diagnosis still requires appropriate criteria and no better explanation.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult has acute myelitis with a long central cord lesion and AQP4-IgG detected by an appropriate assay. What is the best educational interpretation?

options.text: That pattern is compatible with AQP4-positive NMOSD and should not be casually labeled MS.
The lesion proves MS because it is spinal.
AQP4-IgG is specific to MOGAD.
The result removes the need to assess alternative explanations.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AQP4-IgG plus a core clinical syndrome supports NMOSD under consensus criteria, with appropriate exclusion of alternatives. A long lesion is a warning against defaulting to MS.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which approach best reflects proposed MOGAD criteria?

options.text: A positive result alone establishes disease regardless of phenotype.
Require a compatible acquired CNS demyelinating syndrome, MOG-IgG assessed with an appropriate cell-based assay, supportive clinical context and exclusion of alternatives.
Use CSF-only MOG antibody as the universal screening test.
MOGAD is another name for AQP4-positive NMOSD.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The proposed international criteria center on a compatible phenotype and MOG-IgG with cell-based assay, while excluding MS and other mimics; criteria require validation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with suspected relapse reports worsening during fever from a urinary infection. What is the key first distinction?

options.text: Call it a new inflammatory relapse based only on worsening.
Evaluate for infection/other triggers and distinguish pseudo-relapse from new inflammatory activity.
Increase long-term DMT immediately.
Assume progression independent of relapse activity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Intercurrent illness can transiently worsen prior deficits; assess trigger and objective new neurologic activity before classifying the event.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes MS DMT decisions?

options.text: One agent is best for every patient.
Choices balance disease activity, evidence, comorbidity, safety, reproductive goals and patient preferences; check current labeling and monitoring guidance.
DMTs treat only fatigue.
Treatment selection can be made without monitoring.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Treatment decisions are individualized, shared and safety-aware; current therapies/labels evolve. This is an educational principle, not a prescription.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a patient with a compatible optic neuritis syndrome, why should MOG-IgG not be ordered as indiscriminate screening?

options.text: Because MOGAD cannot affect the optic nerve.
Because pretest probability and phenotype affect interpretation and false-positive/low-context results can mislead.
Because the antibody has no relationship to demyelinating disease.
Because all MS patients are MOG-IgG positive.

practiceQuestions.rationale: International panel criteria emphasize compatible syndrome and assay context; testing all patients without selection risks misinterpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is an appropriate use of a public de-identified teaching case from a third-party educational book labeled All Rights Reserved?

options.text: Download/repost the MRI into a new course.
Link learners to the source and do not copy/rehost images without permission.
Remove the watermark and modify the case.
Assume free-to-view means open license.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free viewing is not reuse permission. Link out and comply with the source’s rights notice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees MRI brain white matter hyperintensities in an older adult with vascular risk factors. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Apply MS criteria without regard to age or comorbidities.
Use the revised criteria’s context-sensitive approach, weigh alternative diagnoses and avoid diagnosing from nonspecific lesions alone.
Treat every lesion as dissemination in space.
Skip neurologic localization.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2024 criteria provide guidance for older adults and comorbidities; typical syndrome, specific lesion features and exclusion of alternatives matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: What best characterizes the MGB fellowship from its current official page?

options.text: It is an ACGME MS subspecialty residency that guarantees board eligibility.
Its public page labels it non-GME; it offers separate clinical and clinical-research tracks, with the clinical track described as 1–2 years and research track 2–3 years.
It is a generic directory label only with no described clinics.
It is a pediatric combined fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official program page explicitly marks the opportunity Non-GME and describes separate adult tracks, prerequisites, curriculum allocation and different duration ranges.
